title: Man loses weight eating nothing but a certain food for 25 days — and paid a price
excerpt:
New Jersey resident and content creator Tim Donahue reflects on his experiment consuming food exclusively from Sweetgreen for 25 days and the physical, financial and logistical impact he felt.

A New ...
body_text:
New Jersey resident and content creator Tim Donahue reflects on his experiment consuming food exclusively from Sweetgreen for 25 days and the physical, financial and logistical impact he felt.

A New Jersey man ate nothing but certain foods from a fast-casual chain for 25 days — an experiment that left him nine pounds lighter and craving a slice of pizza.

Tim Donahue, a 27-year-old Hoboken resident who works in advertising in New York City, documented his challenge as a modern-day spin on Morgan Spurlock's 2004 documentary "Super Size Me," he told Fox News Digital.

But instead of eating McDonald's for a month, Donahue wanted to see what would happen if he exclusively ate at a chain on the opposite end of the fast-food spectrum.

AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS

"I think it felt the furthest possible opposite of McDonald's," Donahue said of choosing Sweetgreen.

The idea also came from watching his health-conscious co-workers routinely order Sweetgreen for lunch while he showed up with fast food.

Tim Donahue of Hoboken, New Jersey, challenged himself to eat nothing but salad bowls for 25 days. (Tim Donahue)

"Everyone inside my office is very healthy, and they were getting Sweetgreen bowls every single day for lunch," Donahue said. "I myself would go pick up a fast-food burger and everyone would razz and make fun of me."

Donahue originally intended to make his experiment last for 30 days, but there was a practical problem.

EATING 5 FRUITS AND VEGETABLES A DAY MAY NOT BE ENOUGH FOR HEART HEALTH, STUDY FINDS

"I wanted to do 30, but if you try to look at your calendar and try to fit [it into] any 30-day window, there was always a wedding, a work trip, a reason why I couldn't do 30," he said. "I said, 'You know what, it's either going to get done with 25 days or I'm never going to it done.'"

His primary rule was simple: Whatever he consumed had to be available on Sweetgreen's menu, although he made an exception for black coffee.

Donahue told Fox News Digital he would typically eat fast food for lunch while his co-workers ate Sweetgreen bowls. (Tim Donahue)

And while Sweetgreen offers more than salads, Donahue tried to keep the experiment centered on its bowls.

By the third day, he said, there was little chance of turning back.

Donahue didn't begin the challenge expecting to lose weight, but by the end, the number on his scale had dropped by about nine pounds.

He also found a clear favorite on the menu.

AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY

"I was rocking with the hot honey chicken bowl," he said. "I was getting that all the time."

Donahue said the variety made eating from the same restaurant for nearly a month easier than one might expect. The bigger challenge, he said, was arranging his life around the experiment.

Donahue said he lost about nine pounds during his 25-day personal experiment. (Tim Donahue)

"The most challenging aspect of the project was not the food, it was the logistics," he said.

Meals had to be planned around the store's operating hours. Going out with friends meant skipping drinks and potentially bringing a salad along. Even dates with his girlfriend took a back seat.

One thing Donahue doesn't recommend about his experiment today is the price tag.

"You can cook at home and make a salad at home and spend a significantly smaller amount of money," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Donahue said he offset some of the expense by deciding not to spend money on alcohol or other restaurant meals during the challenge. But, he admitted, it was a "very expensive" project.

"Out of pocket, this is not a sustainable thing to do over groceries," he said.

Donahue also emphasized that Sweetgreen didn't pay him to conduct the experiment.

Donahue said the hot honey chicken bowl was his go-to menu item. (Tim Donahue)

The company subsequently embraced his idea, Donahue said.

"His video inspired us to launch our own 30-day Sweetgreen challenge," Nicolas Jammet, Sweetgreen's co-founder and chief concept officer, told Fox News Digital. "We put out an open call for 30 participants to eat only Sweetgreen for 30 days and document how they feel throughout, and we already received hundreds of applications."

After 25 days of salad bowls, Donahue headed to his favorite neighborhood pizzeria.

"A cheese pizza after a month of salads was incredibly well-deserved," he said.

Donahue's first meal after ending his 25-day challenge was a slice of pizza. (Tim Donahue)

The sudden return to heavier food didn't sit particularly well.

"It did make me feel quite sick because it's a shock to your system," Donahue said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Despite dropping weight and saying he experienced benefits, including more energy, Donahue isn't presenting his experiment as nutritional advice.

He stressed that he isn't a doctor or nutritionist and didn't undertake the challenge to tell others how they should eat.

"The experiment was largely a fun filmmaking journey for me," he said. "I would never prescribe this to someone."

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

title: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle feeding the 'publicity machine' despite privacy demands: expert
excerpt: King Charles confirms Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not return to royal duties. A letter sent on behalf of the King explains their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and the...
body_text:
King Charles confirms Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not return to royal duties. A letter sent on behalf of the King explains their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and they are now akin to private citizens.

Sources close to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are "pushing back" after King Charles issued new guidance on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's positions now that they are back in the United Kingdom.

King Charles issued guidance claiming that Harry and Markle are "akin to private citizens" via a letter issued by the Lord Chamberlain on Sept. 7. Sources told People magazine that Harry and Markle are "public figures" and that if Harry and Markle were private citizens, the Lord Chamberlain "would not have needed to issue a letter of formal guidance."

"Members of the public know who they are. The idea that they can live a normal, ‘private’ life is sadly not realistic," the source added.

King Charles issued a letter declaring Prince Harry and Meghan Markle private citizens after their return to the U.K. (Getty Images)

Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," addressed the "not realistic" claim by the source and told Fox News Digital that the "private citizen" guidance just means that they do not represent the king.

KING CHARLES DRAWS ‘LINE IN THE SAND’ WITH PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE AFTER COUPLE CAUGHT OFF GUARD: EXPERT

"I want to push back on this argument coming from People Magazine and sources close to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle that it's somehow unrealistic for the Sussexes to live as private citizens. Being a private citizen does not mean you're anonymous. It simply means you don't represent the king. The jobs you accept and the responsibilities you take, you take them on as yourself, not the crown," Schofield began.

"In my opinion, you can't repeatedly feed the publicity machine and then complain about a lack of privacy."

Schofield drew a comparison between Princess Anne's children – Zara Tindall and Peter Phillips. Princess Anne is Queen Elizabeth's only daughter and the sister of King Charles. She chose not to give her two kids royal titles at birth.

"They're recognizable, have commercial interests, attend major royal family events, but they do not represent the monarch, yet they have both successfully built lives outside of the working institution. Harry and Meghan could pursue a quieter life, a life like Zara and Peter. They choose not to. In my opinion, you can't repeatedly feed the publicity machine and then complain about a lack of privacy," she said.

Schofield argued that the king’s clarification was necessary as Harry and Markle’s public profile has become increasingly intertwined with the controversies surrounding them.

MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK RETURN POSES PALACE CONTROL ‘NIGHTMARE,’ EXPERT WARNS

"Prince Harry is classified as a non-working member of the royal family whose position is akin to a private citizen. Of course, Harry and Megan are famous. Nobody's disputing that, but where does their fame end and infamy begin? Fame can inspire people to invest in you emotionally and financially. Infamy means people know your name because controversy follows you," she began.

Meghan Markle, Prince Harry and King Charles in 2018. (Getty Images)

Schofield continued, "And after years of feuds, lawsuits, and relationships that deteriorate, I think it's fair to ask how much of the Sussex's enormous public profile today is driven by admiration and how much is driven by controversy, which is precisely why the king has every reason to make their status crystal clear."

Ian Pelham Turner, royal broadcaster, disagrees with Charles's stance on labeling his son and his wife as private citizens.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Harry is the son of a king. He has prominence in Britain. Thus, whether William likes it or not the King should decide not to weakly disenfranchise his second son," Turner said. "He is a billionaire with vast fortunes. Pay for his son’s full security rather than looking like an Ebenezer Scrooge after."

Sources close to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle told People that they are having security concerns. (WireImage/Getty Images)

He continued, "Although some royals still live in Dickens times, we are actually in the 21st century. How would the King feel if a second tragedy happens in his lifetime, first Diana, and potentially Harry and his family?"

Private citizens are not granted security like members of the royal family are.

Richard Fitzwilliams, royal commentator, told Fox News Digital that Charles' letter, declaring Harry and Markle private citizens, is a "total mess."

"The current situation with the King’s letter about their status and the Sussexes response is a total mess. The raising of the security issue which, in the Sussexes view, is a further example of the risks they face, was, in fact, highlighting the incompetence on their part as no proper recce [reconnaissance] has been done during term by their team," Fitzwilliams said.

Prince Harry is King Charles' second son. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

Fitzwilliams argued that the king's letter was a "slap on the wrist" for Meghan and Harry, proving his lack of trust for the former senior royals.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"The King’s letter restated the facts without giving them much of a chance to 'clarify' things. It was clearly intended as a slap on the wrist and evidence that the King didn’t trust them. Unfortunately, nothing is going to stop matters becoming a circus, with royal engagements overshadowed by what they get up to," he said.

As for what's to come, the royal experts are stumped.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle returned to the U.K. six years after leaving for California. (Getty Images)

"It is simply impossible to anticipate the way this may go. It is only clear that, whatever their motives and mistakes, the Sussexes are news whatever they do. That strengthens their hand because it gives them a very high profile. This has nothing to do with the rights and wrongs of any issues involved," Fitzwilliams said.

Schofield explained that Markle and Harry are "unpredictable."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Harry and Megan are unpredictable. The palace can't have governments, charities, businesses, even members of the public wondering whether their activities somehow carry the endorsement of the crown. It doesn't. They don't. King Charles is saying, absolutely not," she said.

Since marrying in 2018 and making their royal exit in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been attempting to carve out their own independent roles outside of the monarchy. (Joshua Sammer/Getty Images)

Schofield continued, "Harry spent years insisting that he wanted independence from the institution. Independence means you don't get to demand the privileges or the authority or the special treatment afforded to people who stayed and did the job. It's the king who determines who represents the crown, not Prince Harry, not Megan Markle, and certainly not anonymous sources briefing People Magazine. Harry wanted his freedom from the system. He got it, but freedom from the system also means accepting that you no longer have a seat at the table."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Archewell and Buckingham Palace for comment.

Janelle Ash is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital covering Hollywood, celebrity culture and breaking entertainment news through exclusive reporting, interviews and in-depth storytelling.

title: Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
excerpt:
Nearly 90% of children in federal custody being directed to GOP-controlled state that has unlicensed facilities and low legal representation rates

The Trump administration has started sending a major...
body_text:
Nearly 90% of children in federal custody being directed to GOP-controlled state that has unlicensed facilities and low legal representation rates

The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.

Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.

This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.

Federal officials’ sudden shift toward ushering these vulnerable kids to the Republican-controlled, deeply conservative state for no publicly stated reason has alarmed immigrants’ rights advocates amid concerns about their treatment and access to due process under US laws.

Experts who spoke to the Guardian fear the advent of a mass apprehension campaign – forcing immigrant children from their communities within the country’s interior to gather them in Texas to ultimately pack them onto repatriation flights, which often leave from areas along the US’s southern border.

“We’re thinking about congregating children in facilities in Texas, where there are less attorneys, where it’s one of the harshest jurisdictions, you know, in the country with regard to immigration judges and how they handle cases. And it’s close to the border, where they can just get planes,” said Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director at the Arizona-based legal service non-profit, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project.

She added that these facilities could be “a deportation churn out factory that has attorneys in name but not real representation”.

Unaccompanied immigrant kids, who often come to the US fleeing abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harms, regularly cross the US-Mexico border and enter the custody of ORR, which is legally tasked with their welfare, not the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency.

There were more than 1,800 kids in ORR’s care nationally at the end of July, scattered among shelters, foster care and secure facilities across the country. Yet already, more than 60% of those still detained with ongoing immigration court proceedings are now believed to be living in Texas, compared with fewer than half in June.

ORR did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.

The processing to Texas is occurring despite the state’s GOP-dominated government refusing to provide state licensing for ORR care providers, a policy that hasn’t stopped the facilities from operating there, but has meant less child welfare oversight and protections for kids.

“Texas is very sympathetic to the Trump administration, at least the governor and the Republican legislature. And so I think the Trump administration knows that not only will there be no pushback from the state government and from the governor, but that people like Governor Greg Abbott are willing accomplices,” Veronica Escobar, a Democratic congresswoman from west Texas, told the Guardian in a phone interview this week.

Meanwhile, many of the kids – from toddlers to teenagers – are navigating the US’s byzantine immigration laws mostly without attorneys. Already, only 31.7% of children in ORR custody with active immigration court proceedings nationally have had a notice of legal representation filed in their cases. Kids held in Texas are faring even worse, with 17.2% in Houston, 18.6% in El Paso and just 8.7% in San Antonio having a legal representation form filed on their behalf, bklg.org’s research found.

“There needs to be far more oversight and representation, for children especially. These kids deserve lawyers,” Escobar said.

At the same time, ORR officials have alarmed advocates by seeking multiple contracts for “emergency influx facilities” of up to 3,000 beds – despite the fact that such facilities can only open when the agency’s operational capacity reaches 85% or higher for multiple days, and ORR’s shelter and foster care network, by its own count, is operating at about 27% capacity.

“Who are they planning to fill those facilities with?” Avila-Cimpeanu asked. “Our fear is huge mass internal apprehension of children.”

Plans for such facilities were first reported by the Independent last month.

At a recent roundtable presentation for roughly 120 stakeholders, ORR officials said the contracts would potentially give the administration “the capability to rapidly respond to any surges at the border of unaccompanied alien children”, according to a transcript of the meeting shared with the Guardian.

But encounters with unaccompanied children at the south-west border have been exceptionally low over the last year and a half. Still, officials pushed for an aggressive timeline, with only 90 days for a facility to become fully operational after a contract is awarded.

“That’s fast and you’re like: ‘I don’t know if I can do that.’ I think it’s very feasible. That is the intent of where we need to be,” said Tony Canales, a branch chief at ORR’s division of acquisition requirements, according to the transcript.

“We’re looking to see whatever you got. I mean, if it’s a permanent facility, if it’s temporary buildings, if it’s a site that is blank that you plan on building on, whatever the case may be. We will definitely look at it and take [it] into consideration,” Canales told the attendees.

The presentation specified that any shelter would require an 8-ft high perimeter fence.

Although officials did not specify a location for such emergency influx facilities, many of the stakeholders closed in on Texas while asking questions.

Officials also said the chosen contractors would be responsible for providing legal services, which could present a serious conflict of interest given that attorneys tasked with representing kids would now be dependent on ORR.

For critics of the second Trump administration, the emergency influx facilities raise the spectre of a worst case scenario, with large-scale detentions for immigrant children in communities across the country, given that there is no apparent current need for the massive shelters otherwise.

“The way that a country and a government treats its children and children in their custody is a direct representation of the level of morality or immorality of that government and those individuals,” Escobar said. “And so it is shameful the way that this administration has chosen to treat children.”

title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
excerpt:
The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility

Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to s...
body_text:
The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility

Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.

The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.

Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.

Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.

Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.

They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.

JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.

The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.

Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.

That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.

In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.

And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.

The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

title: Psychosis evidence changes everything in Clancy judge's other killer mom case: retired judge
excerpt: Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu explains why the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling means a future jury could hear thousands of psychiatric records excluded from Latarsha Sanders' firs...
body_text:
Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu explains why the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling means a future jury could hear thousands of psychiatric records excluded from Latarsha Sanders' first murder trial.

Judge William Sullivan, who drew national attention earlier this month after declaring a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder case, also presided over another closely watched child-killing trial that a retired Massachusetts judge says would look dramatically different if retried.

The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court last month vacated the murder convictions of Brockton mother Latarsha Sanders, ruling jurors were improperly prevented from seeing psychiatric records central to her insanity defense and ordering a new trial.

"They ordered a new trial which will fundamentally change the way the case is going to be tried," retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital.

LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN

Latarsha Sanders appears in Plymouth Superior Court during her 2018 murder trial in Brockton, Mass. Massachusetts' highest court later vacated her convictions and ordered a new trial. (Marc Vasconcellos /The Enterprise via AP, Pool)

Sullivan, who presided over Sanders' 2022 trial and later sentenced her to two concurrent life terms without parole, has returned to the national spotlight following the closely watched Clancy trial, which ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked over whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children. Like Sanders, Clancy admitted killing her children but argued she lacked criminal responsibility because of mental illness.

"There is no doubt the defendant committed these incomprehensible crimes," Justice David Gaziano wrote for the unanimous court in Sanders' case. "The sole issue before a Superior Court jury was whether she lacked criminal responsibility."

LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL

The justices concluded Sanders was entitled to a new trial because jurors never saw medical records documenting diagnoses and treatment of mental illness that were relevant to the only issue disputed at trial: whether she lacked criminal responsibility.

Lu said the ruling does far more than simply order another trial.

"Thousands of pages of mental health records will be admitted ... and the jury's gonna get it all," he said.

Judge William Sullivan speaks during Lindsay Clancy's trial on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

Lu cautioned against judging Sullivan's decision with the benefit of hindsight.

"The trial judge did an excellent job ... but now I'm a great Monday morning quarterback just like everybody else," Lu said, explaining that the evidentiary issue was unusually difficult before the SJC clarified the law.

Sanders admitted killing her sons, 8-year-old Edson "Marlon" Brito and 5-year-old La'Son Brito, but argued she was legally insane at the time of the attacks.

Her attorneys contended she was suffering from severe mental illness and psychosis, while prosecutors argued she appreciated the wrongfulness of her actions despite bizarre statements she made before and after the killings.

According to evidence summarized by the Supreme Judicial Court, Sanders had become consumed by conspiracy theories involving the Illuminati and expressed fears about voodoo before the killings.

After the deaths, investigators said she gave police multiple conflicting accounts before eventually telling detectives the stabbings were part of a "ritual" tied to voodoo and the Illuminati.

Lindsay Clancy looks on as jurors enter the courtroom during Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Sept. 4, 2026. (Greg Derr / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

At trial, Sanders' defense called a clinical neuropsychologist who testified she was "grossly psychotic" at the time of the killings and suffered from a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder.

The expert based that opinion in part on thousands of pages of psychiatric treatment records from prison and a state psychiatric hospital.

Those are the records Lu said a future jury would likely hear if prosecutors pursue another trial.

The Supreme Judicial Court said that was an error, concluding the excluded records documented repeated observations of paranoia, hallucinations, delusional thinking and schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses that formed the medical foundation of Sanders' defense.

"We hold that the exclusion of the MCI-Framingham and WRCH medical records documenting the defendant's post-arrest diagnoses or treatment of mental illness ... impermissibly stripped the sole defense 'of the medical foundation that supported it,'" the court wrote. "The defendant is entitled to a new trial."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Lu said the opinion should not be interpreted as a determination that Sanders was legally insane or wrongly convicted. Instead, he described it as the resolution of a difficult evidentiary question that changes what evidence jurors would be permitted to consider if the case is retried.

During oral arguments before the Supreme Judicial Court, Sanders' attorney, Robert Shaw, argued the trial judge's exclusion of medical evidence deprived his client of "a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense," FOX 25 in Boston reported.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Melissa Johnson countered that Sanders showed no documented psychotic behavior for months after the killings and that the records were properly excluded, the station reported.

The justices also addressed two issues that would likely shape any future trial.

First, they said prosecutors could refer to Sanders describing herself as "evil" because the statements were relevant to whether she appreciated the moral wrongfulness of her actions, so long as the argument remained tied to that legal issue rather than serving as a personal attack.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

However, the court found prosecutors improperly suggested Sanders may have borrowed elements of her story from episodes of "Law & Order: SVU," ruling there was no evidence supporting that theory.

The ruling vacates Sanders' convictions and sends the case back to Plymouth Superior Court for a new trial.

An overturned conviction does not clear Sanders of the charges, Lu said.

"It just means you have to do it all over again," he said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Sullivan, Sanders' attorney and the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office for comment.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

title: Iranian actor Laheh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speech
excerpt: Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women of ...
body_text:
Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women of Iran’

An Iranian actress who won the best newcomer award at the Venice film festival has come under severe attack from the country’s authorities and state media after highlighting the plight of women in Iran in her acceptance speech.

Laleh Marzban last Saturday won the best actress award in the Orizzonti sidebar competition for emerging talent, for her role in Mohsen Gharaei’s Falling House, a film revolving around three generations of women who are incarcerated in their own home by the family’s father.

At the awards gala, Marzban dedicated her prize to “the women of my country who have paid the highest price for even the smallest measure of freedom”. Speaking in Farsi, she added that Iranians were experiencing some of the most difficult days of their lives but should not lose hope.

On Thursday, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution, a conservative-dominated government body appointed by Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement condemning Marzban’s speech as “presenting a one-sided narrative of Iran’s proud society”.

Referring only to “recent statements and behaviour made at the Venice film festival”, it said reducing Iranian women to “the stereotypes desired by western circles […] is not in line with the awareness-raising mission and social commitment of art”.

The statement has come on the back of a raft of similarly worded attacks in state-affiliated Iranian media, some of which called for the actress to be disciplined by the regime.

Zahra Chekhmaghi, a journalist and presenter associated with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), called Marzban “a two-faced person, […] self-interested, hypocritical, despicable and miserable”, while another IRIB-affiliated media personality, actress Zhila Sadeghi, criticised Marzban for not dedicating her speech instead to the children killed in a US missile strike on an elementary school in Minab on 28 February.

On state TV IRIB, a Qu’ran expert said the actress had been “deceived by the enemy” and called on the government to not let her work in Iran. Another news agency, Student News Network (SNN), urged the ministry of culture to not let Marzban back into the country.

The Iranian reaction to Gharaei’s film and Marzban’s speech appears to mirror the pushback against another film that premiered on the Lido this year, Guardian-produced documentary NAZA, about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.

Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said this week he would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating a campaign against NAZA’s directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Gharaei’s Falling House thematises the collapse of traditional patriarchal family structures in Iran, and men’s efforts to keep them in place by force. Marzban plays twentysomething Ensi, who announces to her family her plans to leave the country and pursue a modelling career in Turkey. In a desperate effort to assert his authority, her father Rashid (Farhad Aslani) locks Ensi and the other female members of the household in their rooms.

Asked after Falling House’s Venice premiere how the film would be received in Iran, Marzban said: “This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective,” she said.

“I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.”

title: Russia’s parliamentary election: Who’s on the ballot, and why it matters
excerpt: Russians head to the polls from Friday to Sunday to elect members of the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, in the first parliamentary election to be held since the country launched i...
body_text:
Russians head to the polls from Friday to Sunday to elect members of the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, in the first parliamentary election to be held since the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The vote comes as Russians face a slowing economy as well as Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries and warehouses far from the front line.

United Russia, the governing party that backs President Vladimir Putin, is expected to keep its dominant position.

The authorities are presenting the election as a chance for voters to have their say. Critics argue that with no genuine opposition on the ballot, the result is largely settled in advance.

So why are the elections worth watching? Here is what you need to know:

Starting Friday and lasting through Sunday, Russians will elect members of the lower house, the State Duma.

They will also cast ballots in local elections.

Voters in 11 regions will elect their governors, and 39 regions will elect members of regional legislatures.

Voting is spread over three days to boost turnout among the 111 million eligible voters and includes areas Russia occupies in Ukraine. Electronic voting is allowed.

Half of the Duma’s 450 seats are filled by party lists and the other half are contested in single-ballot races.

Russia’s governing party, formed in 2001 from a merger of pro-Kremlin parties, has backed Putin and dominated the parliament ever since.

United Russia won more than two-thirds of the Duma’s seats in the 2021 election. It is again poised to dominate the body.

The party’s list is led by political heavyweights: Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Russia’s top diplomat for 22 years, and Sergei Sobyanin, Moscow’s powerful mayor.

In an apparent bid to add fresh faces to what is widely seen as a party of bureaucrats, its third-highest-ranking official is war correspondent Yevgeny Poddubny, who was badly wounded by a Ukrainian drone.

Members of United Russia have pledged to back the war effort and Putin’s maximalist goals in what the Kremlin calls the “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Alongside United Russia, other “systemic opposition” parties that vote in sync with the government on key issues are also expected to remain.

The liberal Yabloko Party, the only registered political party that opposes the war, was initially on the ballot, but the Supreme Court ordered it removed in August.

It cited, among other reasons, that the antiwar stance was akin to seeking the violation of Russia’s territorial integrity. Yabloko now runs only single-ballot races.

The Communist Party has been a leading force in the Federal Assembly since the 1990s, led for more than three decades by 82-year-old Gennady Zyuganov, a former Soviet official.

Throughout Putin’s rule of more than a quarter-century, the Communists have criticised some aspects of government policy but carefully avoided any criticism of him. They steadfastly support the war in Ukraine.

Alexander Bratersky, a political analyst and independent journalist, told Al Jazeera that the race for second place is worth watching.

If the Communist Party nab second, it would “suggest voters are angry about economic hardship and falling living standards”.

The Liberal Democratic Party, an ultranationalist force that has been a significant presence in the legislature since the early 1990s, will also likely retain some influence in the Duma.

Like the Communists, it staunchly supports the war and boasts of having multiple veterans as members.

Other smaller parties round out the ballot.

The party known as A Just Russia has been on Russia’s political scene for 20 years. A social-democratic party, it competes with the Communists for older and middle-aged voters nostalgic for the Soviet past, and it supports the war in Ukraine.

The New People Party was founded shortly before the last parliamentary election in 2021, seeking to position itself as a liberal voice representing younger voters and technocrats. It won just more than 5 percent of the vote, allowing it to form a small faction.

Bratersky described the party as “a liberal-leaning party backed by some Kremlin people who are more technocratic and more pro-peace”.

He said it appeals to the “middle-class audience”, and after the Kremlin banned Yabloko, it has been viewed as its substitute.

“So, if they come third with a good number of votes, this is a sign that those who are antiwar used them as their legal avatar,” he said.

Other parties seeking seats include Communists of Russia, a small rival of the main Communist Party; the Party of Pensioners; the Green Party; the Party of Direct Democracy; and the Motherland Party.

While these elections may seem routine, the fact that they are the first since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is what makes them important, Bratersky told Al Jazeera.

He said that Putin has linked the elections to support for the war: Endorsing United Russia at its party congress in August, Putin said the party’s duty was “to do everything for victory” in the war in Ukraine.

“This shows that the Kremlin is a bit worried since the elections are the only legal way to show disrespect for the Kremlin,” Bratersky said. “Even Putin’s core fans hate United Russia as a corrupt force.”

Since Putin first came to power in 2000, United Russia has won every Duma election, usually by a wide margin.

The results have repeatedly been disputed.

In 2011, allegations of vote-rigging set off the largest street protests of Putin’s rule.

After the 2021 vote, independent monitors and statisticians said the party’s real support was far lower than the official count.

The authorities have rejected claims of widespread fraud. Opposition parties and critics of the war have increasingly been kept off the ballot.

title: South Korea says US-North Korea talks possible, rules out Hormuz deployment
excerpt: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Friday that United States President Donald Trump wants dialogue with Pyongyang and confirmed Seoul will not be deploying troops to intervene militarily in ...
body_text:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Friday that United States President Donald Trump wants dialogue with Pyongyang and confirmed Seoul will not be deploying troops to intervene militarily in the Iran war.

“Trump clearly ⁠wants dialogue ⁠with North ⁠Korea,” Lee said on Friday.

He added that while such talks are uncertain, they are not impossible.

South Korea was continuing “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between North Korea and the US.

“The resumption of North Korea-US dialogue would be far easier than resuming inter-Korean dialogue,” he said, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.

Trump, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in his first term, said he plans to meet Kim later this year.

The US president said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.

Seoul has assessed that Pyongyang has about 80-120 nuclear warheads.

North Korea, which has secured critical backing from Russia in recent years, did not clearly respond to Trump.

Inter-Korean relations reached a high in 2018 but deteriorated after talks between Kim and Trump collapsed in February 2019.

On Thursday, a court in Seoul ordered North Korea to pay roughly $32.5m for blowing up the Inter-Korean Liaison Office building in 2020. The office was intended to improve relations on the peninsula but was destroyed amid rising tensions between the neighbours.

South Korea is working to strengthen relations with other regional partners. The first-ever presidential summit between Seoul and five Central Asian states was held on Wednesday, aiming to establish deeper economic engagement with the Russian-allied countries.

Despite growing pressure from the US, Lee reiterated three times that South Korea will not deploy troops to the Strait of Hormuz.

“Let it be clear. There will be no dispatch of troops that will lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war,” Lee said.

The South Korean government found itself at odds with large parts of Korean society as protests broke out in recent weeks opposing a potential deployment of South Korean military assets to the Strait of Hormuz.

Lee added that South Korea will “carry out the minimum necessary activities” to protect its own merchant ships and oil shipping routes.

title: Australia to detain tourists who overstay visas amid immigration crackdown
excerpt:
Australia will begin detaining visa overstayers as part of a broader immigration crackdown, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced.

The Australian Border Force will expand its team by 100 complia...
body_text:
Australia will begin detaining visa overstayers as part of a broader immigration crackdown, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced.

The Australian Border Force will expand its team by 100 compliance officers, who will work to detain or encourage the departure of roughly 77,000 people currently living in Australia without a valid visa, Burke said Thursday.

He said the policy was designed to reintroduce consequences for overstaying.

“Before 2015, we had a routine process in Australia for overstayers where, when people had overstayed a visa, we would bring people into detention centres … and within a few weeks they would organise their own flight and leave,” Burke announced at the National Press Club.

To aid the operation, 250 new detention beds will be created, including the possible use of a former quarantine facility in Melbourne.

He rejected comparisons to the United States’ hardline Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, saying, “This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries.”

Burke also said the government would clamp down on “visa hopping”, a system that Canberra alleges is when foreigners who are already in Australia move from one type of temporary visa to another to extend their stay.

A new “No Further Stay” provision would prevent people arriving on tourist visas from lodging new applications once inside the country, while international students would be required to advance their qualifications when seeking a new study visa, closing off the option of jumping between courses at low-level institutions to extend their stay.

Burke said separate legislation would be needed to curb a significant caseload of people making what he called “disingenuous” asylum claims to prolong their time in the country.

Rights groups pushed back, and the Human Rights Law Centre warned the change could deter exploited undocumented workers from reporting abuse.

Australia’s governing Labor Party has denied that its tightened visa rules are a response to the growing popularity of the far-right One Nation Party, which has emerged as one of the country’s most popular parties in 2026.

Australia remains one of the world’s most popular tourist destinations, drawing millions of annual visitors with its beaches, wildlife and cities, while also relying heavily on international students and working-holiday visa holders as a major source of migration and economic activity.

The overstayer population has grown steadily, from about 64,000 in 2016 to more than 77,000 in 2026, even as net overseas migration has fallen.

title: MPs urge ministers to break off Thames Water talks with US hedge funds
excerpt:
Efra committee calls for emergency legislation enabling government to take public control of the company

Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-par...
body_text:
Efra committee calls for emergency legislation enabling government to take public control of the company

Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company.

Adding their voices to demands that the prime minister takes public control of the company, which has debts of £20bn and is being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors, the MPs said in a report that ministers should consider emergency legislation to take control of its financial affairs to stabilise the company.

Alistair Carmichael, the chair of the environment, food and rural affairs committee (Efra), said it was unbelievable that the special administration regime (SAR) for insolvent or failing water companies could not be triggered for Thames Water on performance grounds alone.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has suggested that an SAR – effectively temporary public control – cannot be triggered under the current law because of the way the US hedge funds that bought Thames Water’s debt have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its liabilities.

The report said Ofwat and the government should withdraw from negotiating with the consortium of distressed-debt specialists who lacked the proper expertise to turn around a vital public service.

Carmichael said the creditors were operating in an opaque way, seeking relief from environmental penalties and dragging out negotiations while reaping millions of pounds in debt interest.

“Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith in it,” he said. “They are sick of seeing their waterways polluted, their bills going up, and drinking water gush through broken pavements while supplies run low. We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joy-riding in the family car.

“The government should reject offers from the company’s creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service. We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds and others has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”

The report said ministers should explore all potential alternative options, including an SAR or using fresh legislation to draw a line under the debacle and restore stability to the sector by putting Thames Water on a sound footing for new buyers.

Carmichael said putting the company into special administration once its money ran out could be the only way to reset its fortunes. “Liabilities that the government will face in the short term may be offset by a future sale of Thames Water once a new buyer can be found,” he said.

The intervention comes after 64 MPs debated a 200,000-strong petition, set up by the campaigner Ash Smith of Windrush Against Sewage Pollution, to hold a referendum on putting the privatised water industry back into public ownership.

MPs on the Efra committee said they were concerned that not enough regulatory due diligence had been carried out on the US-led consortium that bought Thames Water’s debt.

Elliott Investment Management is one of the leading creditors in the group that includes Silver Point Capital, BlackRock and M&G. Elliott’s founder and co-chief executive is Paul Singer, a Trump donor whom Bloomberg has described as “the most feared investor in the world”.

The consortium of hedge funds – known as London & Valley Water – is attempting to take over Thames in a multibillion-pound restructuring. It is seeking relief from environmental fines which could be worth up to £1bn, requesting leniency on environmental measures including pollution, leakage and other performance targets imposed a year ago.

MPs said: “Their demands demonstrate that they will not prioritise the swift turnaround in performance that Thames Water so desperately needs.

“Whilst keeping the company in limbo by drawing out negotiations, these creditors are simultaneously reaping millions in debt interest and fees. We have grave concerns … L&VW is an opaque consortium which is failing to live up to the transparency the public expects of the water sector.”

The committee said it was difficult to see why SAR had not already been instigated for Thames Water. “Thames Water is at the end of the road. The company’s performance and the behaviour of its creditors are unacceptable. Their investment strategies are based on extracting value through debt rather than ensuring long-term success.”

A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “Our enhanced proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water’s complex problems.

“The plan will write off billions of pounds of debt to achieve an investment grade rating and provide £10bn of new capital from experienced investors to improve and upgrade Thames Water’s infrastructure and clean up local rivers.

“All fines Thames Water faces will be paid, all profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.
 “A new board with specialist expertise will oversee Thames Water’s transformation and work tirelessly to drive the turnaround and rebuild trust. We are committed to ensuring Thames Water provides the service that customers and local communities deserve. This group of investors has never been in control of the company and has never received a dividend from Thames Water. They have stepped in to fund a significant revenue shortfall to ensure Thames Water’s record capital investment programme can continue without disruption.”

title: Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules
excerpt:
Switch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressed

The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the ...
body_text:
Switch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressed

The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”.

One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”.

Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-page book, they can add a touch of undeniable class.

Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”.

“Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties.

He called them “little works of art”, and decried those who shunned them while dressing formally. “It looks as if you’re not completely dressed, or you’ve forgotten something,” he said.

On Savile Row, views on ties were mixed. “I don’t think ties are completely dead, they’re just having a down moment,” said Guy Hills, 58, a fashion photographer and owner of Dashing Tweed, who was sauntering down the street in a green tweed suit. Something else was also green: his moustache.

He said his dyed facial hair might be allowed in the House of Lords, and is in support of the relaxed dress code, believing that members have a responsibility to keep up with fashion trends.

“They used to be the driving force of fashion, especially around Savile Row. They would go to their tailors and try to outdo each other. When you stop all that, and it becomes like a living museum, then the whole menswear fashion world stops,” he said.

Hills usually has something around his neck. “I can’t go out without a scarf because it looks too slovenly,” he said. But Thursday afternoon was, unluckily, one of the rare occasions he was without a silk scarf or cravat.

While ties aren’t totally “in”, Hills thinks they could make a comeback. “The younger generation is now getting more interested in sustainability and proper clothing. A tie really finishes a whole outfit off,” he said.

Among the few wearing a tie on Savile Row was Chaand Singh. The 25-year-old, who works in marketing, had decided to wear a navy tie from Next because of an important work meeting. “Dressing up and adding a tie elevates the look,” he said – so much so that he had received compliments from people. “Someone said that I look a bit more sharp today.”

Ties were no longer an office must, said Singh – but he thinks they still have their place. “I’ve got some from the 80s with cool patterns. They’re usually wider and designed when fashion was a bit more experimental,” he said. “I would wear them at work for the right scenario, but casually as well. Some girls even wear ties as belts.”

What do tailors on the Row think? “The House of Lords should be a mirror of society. What better way of doing it than reflecting current trends?” said James Sleater, 45, the owner of Norton & Sons. “Women don’t have to wear ties, and if men have the option, it’s OK by me.”

Sleater said that in the “post-Covid era, there has been a huge decline in neckwear and the number of people wearing ties to the office”, adding that the “relaxation of dress codes is symptomatic of people working several days a week at home”.

Norton & Sons sees people from all walks of life. “Yesterday we had an ex-prime minister and today we’ve got a Hollywood star having a fitting. We also see people wanting a suit for their first job and people celebrating a wedding,” he says. Have these customers shunned ties and other neckwear in droves? Actually, no. “We’re seeing the reversal of this trend,” says Sleater. “We’re selling more neckwear this year than we did in previous years.

“If you’re no longer forced to do something, it almost becomes a pleasure to it,” he adds. “To wear a suit to work when you don’t have to is a joy. When you’re told to do it, you’re almost feeling rebellious and you don’t want to do it.”

People have opted for “more characterful textures rather than just plain silks or bright brash colours”, though Slater sees a limit to a potential neckwear revival. “I don’t see cravats or bow ties coming back,” he said.

As for Lords who can keep their ties at home, some are in favour of the new rules. “In truth, the only people now wearing ties for business purposes are estate agents and funeral directors,” Lord Davies of Brixton, a Labour peer, told the Telegraph. “The tie is disappearing.”

It remains to be seen if Davies’ fellow Lords will heed the message.

title: Sydney woman sentenced for killing and dismembering abusive husband
excerpt:
‘Disposal of the body in this case was as thorough as it was brutal,’ justice Peter Hamill said when sentencing 55-year-old Nirmeen Noufl

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get o...
body_text:
‘Disposal of the body in this case was as thorough as it was brutal,’ justice Peter Hamill said when sentencing 55-year-old Nirmeen Noufl

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A woman who lied to police multiple times to cover up killing and dismembering her abusive husband will spend a further 12 months in jail.

Nirmeen Noufl was sentenced on Friday to at least three years in jail after pleading guilty in August to killing her husband, Mamdouh Noufl, in excessive self-defence while she was being choked and assaulted in their Sydney home.

The 55-year-old has been in custody since her arrest in October 2024, when she was originally charged with murder before prosecutors accepted an admission to the lesser charge. With time served, Noufl will be eligible for parole in October 2027.

Crown prosecutor Mark Hay told the court the disposal of Mamdouh Noufl’s body meant her version of events had to be accepted and a murder charge could not be pursued.

An extremely traumatic childhood followed by severe domestic violence mitigated the seriousness of the mid-2023 killing, but the dismemberment was important to the case, the judge said.

“Disposal of the body in this case was as thorough as it was brutal,” justice Peter Hamill said on Friday.

“The conduct after the killing is remarkable and chilling … and is also relevant to issues such as remorse.”

A key factor in sentencing was the sustained history of abuse she suffered at her husband’s hand, culminating in the attack she said she was experiencing when she stabbed her husband.

“This was a gravely abusive relationship featuring violence, psychological manipulation and coercive control,” the judge said.

Noufl wiped away tears in court as Hamill outlined the circumstances of extreme violence and abuse in her childhood and marriage.

The judge indicated members of Mamdouh Noufl’s family would probably be disappointed with the maximum sentence of six years and nine months.

“I hope all of you understand … there will seem to be a gap between the loss you have suffered forever and the sentence I impose,” the judge said.

Mamdouh Noufl held conservative Islamic views and was controlling of his wife and daughters, according to the agreed facts.

Just days before his death in their Greenacre home, he told his wife he met a woman in Egypt months earlier whom he planned to marry. But he denied Noufl’s request for a divorce.

When he returned home later that day, they got into an argument and he assaulted her, choking her as he pinned her to the ground, Noufl later told psychiatrists.

“All my life … he just treated me like shit, spat at me,” the 55-year-old told a confidante after the killing. “I had enough.”

Noufl dismembered her husband’s body using a saw and disposed of it in multiple garbage bags across south-west Sydney.

His body was never found and her claim that she stabbed him only once in the chest could not be tested.

One of Noufl’s daughters told the court she would uproot her life abroad and return to Australia to help her mother attend psychiatric appointments when she was released.

“If she were to be released tomorrow, I would cancel my flight,” the daughter, who can’t be identified for legal reasons, said.

During sentencing proceedings, different accounts of Mamdouh Noufl’s character emerged from the divided family.
 In a victim impact statement tendered to the court, Khaled Noufal said his uncle was a “shining light”.

“He possessed a rare, pure kindness that touched everyone who crossed his path.”

The nephew vented frustration outside court on Friday, telling reporters his aunt should have received a much lengthier sentence.

Six of the couple’s eight children gave written evidence about the sustained violent abuse their father inflicted on his wife over 22 years of marriage.

“Our family experienced significant turmoil over the years due to the violent actions of my father,” one of the children told the court.

“He would slap her, push her and shove her – even when she was pregnant.”

title: Bills cruise past Lions to christen new home behind Josh Allen's five-touchdown performance
excerpt: The Buffalo Bills play the Detroit Lions tomorrow, and Bills HC Joe Brady said that his team will "Try to put on a clinic" for his first home game at Highmark Stadium. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, an...
body_text:
The Buffalo Bills play the Detroit Lions tomorrow, and Bills HC Joe Brady said that his team will "Try to put on a clinic" for his first home game at Highmark Stadium. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if this is disrespectful to the Lions, what an 0-2 start would mean for the New England Patriots, and if Ben Johnson saying that the Chicago Bears "wanted to score 60" is good or not.

The wait for regular-season football at the Buffalo Bills' new home ended Thursday night, when Highmark Stadium hosted its first regular-season game.

Right on cue, Buffalo's star quarterback Josh Allen orchestrated a picture-perfect first half as the home team raced to a 27-10 halftime lead over the Detroit Lions. Allen threw three touchdown passes and ran for two scores to power the Bills to a 41-31 victory.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Allen recorded the fourth five-touchdown game of his career Thursday, one week after throwing two touchdown passes and running for two more in a 36-31 season-opening win over the Houston Texans.

BUFFALO BILLS' PLAN TO FEATURE CANADIAN ANTHEM AT STADIUM OPENER MET WITH MIXED REACTIONS

A general interior view of Highmark Stadium as fireworks erupt and the Buffalo Bills take the field before an NFL game between the Bills and Detroit Lions on Sept. 17, 2026, in Orchard Park, New York. (Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images)

The $2.1 billion stadium that officially opened last month was built across the street from the Bills' former home.

Allen followed the pregame fireworks celebration with more fireworks of his own by overseeing touchdown drives on each of Buffalo’s first four possessions. Bills running back James Cook had 134 yards rushing and put the game away with a 1-yard TD run with just under three minutes remaining.

Allen’s two rushing touchdowns upped his career total to 83, moving him into a tie for 18th on the NFL list with Jim Taylor. He also picked up his 90th regular-season victory, becoming one of just four quarterbacks to reach that milestone in their first nine seasons.

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) runs with the ball against the Detroit Lions during the first quarter at Highmark Stadium on Sept. 17, 2026, in Orchard Park, New York. (Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images)

The Lions were undone by an injury-depleted defense, and a banged-up offensive line that had difficulty opening holes for Jahmyr Gibbs and protecting Jared Goff.

After rallying from a 21-0 deficit to cut Buffalo’s lead to 34-24, the Lions' offense stalled midway through the fourth quarter. Backed up at their own 10, the Lions went three-and-out and were forced to punt after Goff had two passes tipped by Deone Walker, and Gibbs was stopped for no gain.

Goff finished 26 of 38 for 327 yards and four touchdowns, while Amon-Ra St. Brown had nine catches for 142 yards and two scores. Gibbs scored on an 11-yard catch but was limited to 52 rushing yards, and Sam LaPorta added a 1-yard touchdown reception.

Highmark Stadium is shown before an NFL game between the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions in Orchard Park, New York, on Sept. 17, 2026. (Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images)

Despite being an open-air facility, the Bills' new home was designed to withstand Buffalo’s weather. Underground heating coils keep the natural-grass field from freezing, while roof sensors monitor snowfall and activate the world’s largest stadium snow-melt system.

The new stadium will also shield most fans from the wind with its 360-degree canopy.
