Yemen’s stability is no longer a purely Yemeni matter, but a first line of defence for the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb and for the cohesion of the Arab sphere, with Riyadh and Cairo remaining central pillars in confronting projects of disintegration and fragmentation.

Within this emerging order, the Saudi-Egyptian partnership is becoming a cornerstone of regional security. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s expected visit to Cairo and summit with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi give practical expression to the principle of “collective responsibility”.

Riyadh and Cairo recognise that the security of the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb is not a local matter: it is vital to the Suez Canal and Egyptian economy, and forms strategic and security depth for Saudi Arabia.

By coordinating diplomatic and military action, supporting the full liberation of Yemen and containing the reach of the militias, the two countries are helping shape an autonomous regional security order intended to fill the vacuums left by retreating international powers, protect international navigation and confront shared threats from a position of parity and capacity.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Ninth woman's body found as South African police investigate string of deaths
excerpt:
The latest body was found wrapped in a sheet on the side of the road in Dawn Park

Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months, amid growing concern ...
body_text:
The latest body was found wrapped in a sheet on the side of the road in Dawn Park

Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months, amid growing concern over a string of unexplained deaths east of Johannesburg.

The latest victim was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Dawn Park on Thursday morning, police said. Her identity has not yet been released.

The discovery follows the deaths of eight other women whose bodies have been found since July across Ekurhuleni, a major urban area of Johannesburg.

Several of the women were found partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings, which he said were "causing fear and uncertainty in our communities".

Among the victims was 38-year-old Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo, who disappeared last week after leaving her home for an afternoon run. Her body was found three days later behind a hotel in Kempton Park.

Two other victims have since been identified as Itumeleng Kekana, who had been missing since July, and 38-year-old Dineo Evelyn Motapane, whose body was discovered by the roadside in KwaThema on Tuesday.

The first of the nine bodies was discovered in Kempton Park on 15 July. A suspect was arrested two days later in connection with that case and remains in custody, but police have not linked that suspect to the other deaths.

Further bodies were discovered in August and September, including in Kempton Park, Olifantsfontein, Clayville and KwaThema.

The latest body is of a woman believed to be in her 30s and appeared to have bruises and stab wounds, local media reported.

Police have assembled a multidisciplinary team of detectives, intelligence officers, forensic experts and other specialists to investigate the deaths and establish whether there are links between the cases.

They are also pursuing a person of interest, although they have not disclosed which case or cases that person may be connected to.

"Let's not get emotional, the gloves are off," said Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi on Thursday, adding that the authorities had the capacity to deal with the killings.

Authorities have offered a 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) reward for information that could lead to arrests and have appealed to families with missing relatives to help identify the remaining victims.

The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concern about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.

Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.

Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has cautioned against speculation, saying investigators were dealing with what appeared, at this stage, to be "quite distinct, separate events".

Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, external, on Facebook at BBC Africa, external or on Instagram at bbcafrica, external

title: From Yanbu to Sohar: Tracking Saudi Arabia’s alternative oil routes
excerpt: Saudi Arabia’s oil exports took another blow last week when drone attacks knocked out part of the country’s East-West pipeline, halting oil flow and removing 4-5 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil f...
body_text:
Saudi Arabia’s oil exports took another blow last week when drone attacks knocked out part of the country’s East-West pipeline, halting oil flow and removing 4-5 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil from global supply.

It is unclear how long repairs will take, although The Associated Press estimates three to five weeks, citing two regional officials.

The 1,200km (746-mile) pipeline connects the kingdom’s main oil-producing fields in the east of the country with Yanbu port on the Red Sea coast in the west, allowing Saudi crude to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has largely remained closed since the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28.

As the world’s second-largest oil producer, Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep crude flowing has significant consequences for global energy markets. Al Jazeera asked experts what alternatives remain, how the disruption could affect buyers worldwide, and what it means for the kingdom’s revenues.

Total Saudi crude loadings, which topped 7.5 million bpd in January and February, had fallen to about 2.3 million bpd in August and roughly 2.1 million bpd in the first half of September – a drop of more than 70 percent.

Analysts caution the real loadings figure may run somewhat higher, since shuttle tankers crossing Hormuz with tracking switched off aren’t always captured in vessel data.

Saudi exports are built around two coastal passages – the Gulf in the east, where crude moves out through the Strait of Hormuz, and the Red Sea in the west, where it can travel either north through the Suez Canal and Sumed Pipeline, or south through the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Before the crisis, most Saudi crude left on ships through the Strait of Hormuz, the 39km (24-mile) shipping choke point connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, and the open sea beyond.

Saudi Arabia was exporting about 7-8 million bpd of oil, with most seaborne volumes loading at the terminals of Ras Tanura and Ras al-Ju’aymah, and the former averaging about 5.4 million bpd in 2025.

The route is the most direct and economical way to reach Asia, which buys the bulk of Saudi crude exports.

With the western pipeline route closed and the Red Sea’s southern route hostile, Saudi Arabia has little choice but to push exports back through the Gulf – despite the restrictions, higher costs, and physical risk of attack that come with transiting Hormuz, experts say.

“With the East-West pipeline offline, Saudi’s options are limited. The first is shipping more crude from its Gulf terminals through the Strait of Hormuz, including ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, such as off Sohar in Oman,” according to Rishi Rajanala, research specialist in Oil Americas at LSEG Data & Analytics.

“Gulf producers have already been moving part of their exports this way, but volumes depend on tanker availability, insurance and freight costs, and remain well below pre-war levels.

“The second is drawing on crude already stored on the west coast and at Egypt’s Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir terminals, which can continue to supply Europe through the Sumed Pipeline, but only for as long as stored volumes last. The third is a phased restart of the pipeline itself, depending on the extent of the damage.”

Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipping services company, said transiting back through Hormuz will “further fuel higher freight costs for Middle East exports and create additional inefficiencies”, adding, “we do not know how long Yanbu loadings will be suspended for, but it doesn’t look to be a quick fix.”

One way to reduce that risk is for tankers to go “dark” by switching off their AIS transponders – used in maritime navigation to identify and track vessels – as they transit Omani coastal waters. “They will transit with transponders off and likely coordinate with the US Navy but still face the risk of attack as everyone else does,” Matthews said.

If the outage extends beyond a few weeks, the balance shifts further: Stored volumes would run down, and any crude that cannot move through the Gulf would have to be stored or left unproduced, adding pressure to production levels already well below pre-war volumes in August.

Rahul Choudhary, vice president of Upstream Research at Rystad Energy, an independent energy research company, said Hormuz-route exports increased in September to more than two million bpd in the first two weeks, roughly one million bpd above August.

“We expect Strait of Hormuz exports to rise further in the second half of the month, already evident in Aramco offering additional loadings to Asian refiners out of Sohar. Saudi Arabia can lean further on dark tanker activity in the coming days to offset Yanbu losses,” he added.

Most of Saudi Arabia’s crude is produced in the east, and Aramco’s East-West pipeline links the Ghawar and Abqaiq processing facilities there to Yanbu port on the opposite side of the country.

It was built in 1981, during the Iran-Iraq war, precisely to reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz in a crisis of the kind Saudi Arabia and other Gulf exporters are now facing.

It runs at a maximum capacity of about 7 million bpd.

Crude shipped from Yanbu has two ways to travel onward through the Red Sea – south via Bab al-Mandeb or north via Suez.

Shipments heading south to Asia must pass through the Bab al-Mandeb strait – the second-best route after Hormuz.

But Iran-backed Houthi forces launched a rapid military offensive in September, seizing the Yemeni port of Mocha, the coastal town of Dhubab, and Mayyun Island, and now control the strait. They have also declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia, prohibiting vessels from loading or discharging cargo at Saudi ports.

With the southern exit blocked, tankers wishing to reach Asia must instead travel north.

Oil tankers can pass through the Suez Canal directly, or discharge their cargo at Egypt’s Ain Sokhna terminal on the Red Sea into the Sumed pipeline, which carries it overland across Egypt to a Mediterranean port near Alexandria, where it is reloaded onto tankers bound for Europe.

Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) are too large to transit the canal at full draft – the maximum safe depth when fully loaded – so they instead partially discharge at Ain Sokhna and reload the remaining volume at the Mediterranean terminal before continuing.

According to HSBC Global Investment Research, Aramco had planned a similar “shuttling” operation before Yanbu was suspended, using smaller Suezmax tankers to move crude between Yanbu and Ain Sokhna.

From there, reaching Asian buyers means sailing west through the Strait of Gibraltar and around the Cape of Good Hope – a journey of about 13,140 nautical miles (equivalent to about 24,335km) that dwarfs the roughly 3,370 nautical miles (6,241km), 10-day journey via Hormuz, adding almost a month to the voyage and making shipping far more expensive while tying up tankers for longer.

But some experts expect the East-West pipeline to resume operations sooner, offering hope that Saudi oil exports could return to more sustainable levels.

Choudhary said: “We expect the pipeline to restart within a couple of weeks at a reduced 40-60 percent capacity, flowing around 2.5-3 million bpd. With Saudi likely to prioritise refinery runs, only about 0.5-1 million bpd would be left for export, meaning Yanbu crude exports fall by 2.5-3 million bpd even after a partial restart.

“Part of that gap can be covered by higher Hormuz liftings and increased dark-fleet activity, bringing the net impact on Saudi crude exports down to roughly 1.5-2 million bpd.”

One option conspicuously absent from Saudi planning is trucking – and the maths explains why. The kingdom typically exports 5-7 million bpd. Replacing even a single day’s volume by road would require roughly 25,000 to 35,000 fully loaded tanker trucks, each carrying about 200 barrels.

Lined up bumper-to-bumper, that convoy would stretch nearly 500km (310 miles) – roughly the distance from Riyadh to the nearest coast.

A single VLCC, by comparison, carries about 2 million barrels in one voyage, and the pipeline itself moves millions of barrels daily with minimal manpower – which is why, even with its main export arteries compromised, Saudi Arabia’s fallback plan runs through ships, not roads.

Oil prices have so far been cushioned by stockpiles and releases from strategic reserves, with Brent crude trading at about $70-$90 a barrel in recent months. But the longer regional disruptions continue, the more we may see prices rise, with Brent crude currently trading above $105 a barrel.

“The market is pricing a significant loss of supply, with the length of the outage as the main uncertainty. Saudi authorities have not given a timeline for the repair, and estimates reported so far range from a few days to eight weeks for a full recovery,” Rajanala, the research specialist at LSEG, said.

Saudi Arabia was, until recently, the world’s largest oil exporter.

Its main buyers are Asian and European refiners, including China, which bought 22 percent of Saudi Arabia’s oil, followed by South Korea (14 percent), Japan (13 percent), India (10 percent) and the US (5 percent).

Those buyers are already feeling the shutdown. Cargoes scheduled for European refiners are being cancelled, forcing many companies to look elsewhere for their oil, including turning to the US, North Sea and West Africa.

“Some European refiners with cancelled Saudi cargoes are already sourcing crude from the North Sea and seeking cargoes from the Americas and Central Asia, while Asian buyers are being offered alternative loadings from the Gulf,” Rajanala said.

“The missing barrels are also higher sulphur crude. Saudi grades such as Arab Light and Arab Medium are difficult to replace, like-for-like, because the alternatives available from the US, Kazakhstan and much of the North Sea are generally lower in sulphur content. That puts particular pressure on refiners configured for Middle East crude, many of them in Asia, which takes the largest share of Saudi exports.”

Despite higher oil prices benefitting Saudi Arabia, they are being offset by an inability to physically export at normal volumes.

The government depends heavily on dividends, royalties and taxes from Aramco, with its crude and petroleum products sales accounting for more than half of government revenues, generating 606.5 billion riyals ($162bn) for state coffers in 2025.

Sustained disruption would cut deep into public finances. UBS Research now forecasts the 2026 budget deficit reaching 5 percent of gross domestic product against an original target of 3.3 percent.

Louis Vincent-Gave, from Gavekal Research, an independent research firm, noted that “the bombing of Yanbu, combined with the bombing of the East-West pipeline, and the Houthi takeover of the Bab el-Mandab sea passage, suddenly places large question marks on the ability of Saudi oil to keep flowing through the Red Sea to the rest of the world. And if Saudi Arabia cannot keep pumping oil to the rest of the world, the Saudi government could end up selling assets – US treasuries? Stakes in private equity funds? Artificial intelligence investments? – to pay its immediate bills.”

title: International students, 'visa hoppers' and backpackers targeted in Australia migration crackdown
excerpt:
Australia will cut immigration by cracking down on international students and backpackers, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says

International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will ...
body_text:
Australia will cut immigration by cracking down on international students and backpackers, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says

International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.

Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.

Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.

The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".

For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."

There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.

PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said.

In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.

On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".

Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.

He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year.

Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.

Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.

For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.

New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.

That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100.

Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.

One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.

The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".

In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas  lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas.

Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.

It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.

Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country".

"The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

title: Women in England with incurable breast cancer to get life-extending drug on NHS
excerpt:
Thousands with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will have access to Enhertu after ministers strike deal on price

Thousands of women in England with incurable breast cancer will get access to a life-ex...
body_text:
Thousands with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will have access to Enhertu after ministers strike deal on price

Thousands of women in England with incurable breast cancer will get access to a life-extending drug on the NHS after negotiations over its cost proved successful.

About 1,000 women a year with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will be able to obtain Enhertu from Thursday after ministers and the drug’s makers struck a deal on its price.

About one in seven of the 60,000 new cases of breast cancer diagnosed every year in the UK are HER2-positive.

Clinical trials have shown that Enhertu almost doubled median progression-free survival compared with normal chemotherapy, from 5.1 months to 9.9 months. Median overall survival among people who used it was 23.4 months, compared with 16.8 months among those not on it – a 6.6-month gain.

“This is a momentous day for thousands of people who will now have access to a drug that will give them the opportunity to gain precious time with loved ones”, said Claire Rowney, the chief executive of Breast Cancer Now.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) announced on Thursday that about 1,000 patients a year in England will be eligible to receive the treatment from the NHS after it recommended it for routine use.

Nice, which advises the NHS on whether treatments represent value for money, had previously rejected Enhertu, in July 2024, as too expensive to justify, despite its proven effectiveness.

Rowney hailed “this milestone victory”, which follows two years of determined campaigning by the charity, cancer specialists and women with that form of breast cancer.

The drug has been available since December 2023 in Scotland, which is one of 27 European countries that provide it to patients. Labour ministers, including ex-health secretary Wes Streeting, have been working behind the scenes for some time to add England to that list by brokering a deal on cost. Their efforts were hampered by the drugmakers’ refusal to lower their price.

Nice’s U-turn follows recent renewed negotiations between it, NHS England and Enhertu’s two makers, the pharmaceutical firms AstraZeneca and Daiichi Sankyo. They resulted in what Nice called “a commercial solution” that means the drug is now available in England for the first time.

The freedom that Nice gained in April to recommend that the NHS can spend up to £35,000 a year on a patient’s treatment, up from a previous maximum of £30,000, proved crucial. It has agreed to pay more for Enhertu than it was previously prepared to do. But it is unclear if the drug’s two makers reciprocated by reducing the amount they had been seeking.

“This is hugely positive news for women with secondary breast cancer who will now be offered this life-extending treatment on the NHS,” said Dr Anne Rigg, a consultant medical oncologist who is also NHS England’s national speciality adviser for chemotherapy.

Dr Catherine Elliott, Cancer Research UK’s director of research, said: “Enhertu is a targeted treatment that delivers chemotherapy directly to cancer cells.

“Clinical trial results show that, for people with HER2-low advanced breast cancer whose disease has progressed following treatment, it can help them live longer and delay their cancer from getting worse compared with standard chemotherapy.”

Ministers in Wales and Northern Ireland are likely to implement Nice’s recommendation and make it available there too.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said: “Enhertu can be life-changing and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it.

“It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this, and it follows the changes this government has made to the Nice framework as part of the UK-US pharmaceutical partnership so more people can benefit from cutting-edge treatments.”

title: Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
excerpt:
Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports

The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing...
body_text:
Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports

The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).

That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.

This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.

Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.

But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.

"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.

That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?

For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.

This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans

As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.

I said no surprises. But there have been some.

"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.

The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.

"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."

In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:

Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:

"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"

It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.

"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."

I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.

But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.

One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.

Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.

"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.

"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.

"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."

Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular

For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.

"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."

Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.

The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.

Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.

In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.

The war is front and centre of people's minds here.

Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."

"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."

Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.

"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."

Expectations are low that this election will change much.

"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.

"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

title: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
excerpt:
Austin Tice filed high-profile news reports during the Syrian civil war

US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a mont...
body_text:
Austin Tice filed high-profile news reports during the Syrian civil war

US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal.

A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.

Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic.

But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.

In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time.

His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.

Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice.

Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.

As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them.

We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.

A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed. Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.

But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.

Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?

We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.

He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.

Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.

We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.

The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad.

"Bring him to us," Assad replied, claims Abu Ali.

Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.

But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing.

"He trusts me," Abu Ali recalls the driver saying.

Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says.

Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.

To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.

In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.

On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet.

"Hands down, best birthday ever," he wrote.

Tice's mother Debra has pressed successive US presidents to continue looking for her son

Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.

But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.

Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.

Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening.

According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.

NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says.

Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.

For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.

The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.

They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared.

His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.

But they did give a motive for his betrayal of Tice.

The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions.

According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.

Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum.

Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.

Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.

The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

title: Argentinian judge orders suspension of Falklands oil project
excerpt: An Argentinian judge has ordered the suspension of a British-Israeli oil project near the Falkland Islands in a purely symbolic move as Argentina escalates its claim over the British-administered terr...
body_text:
An Argentinian judge has ordered the suspension of a British-Israeli oil project near the Falkland Islands in a purely symbolic move as Argentina escalates its claim over the British-administered territory.

Wednesday’s interim ruling issued by a court in Argentina’s southernmost province, Tierra del Fuego, follows a lawsuit filed by 1982 war veterans and environmental lawyers earlier this month.

The plaintiffs sought to block Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum from the Sea Lion oilfield, located about 220km (137 miles) from the islands.

The judge ordered the companies to “refrain from initiating, pursuing, carrying out or having carried out any material actions” that would involve drilling, installing infrastructure or extracting hydrocarbons, according to a ruling seen by the AFP news agency.

Additionally, the suspension applies “until such time as the environmental impact assessment procedure has been conducted before the national authority competent in environmental matters”.

The judge gave the parties 10 days to provide information, including details about the status of the project, its contractors and its financiers.

President Javier Milei’s administration has also taken legal action against the project, arguing it violates a United Nations resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute is resolved.

The court order comes just a day after Argentina announced it would file further legal complaints against companies exploring for oil near the islands, intensifying its campaign against businesses operating in the British overseas territory.

Britain and Argentina fought a brief but bitter 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, known to Argentines as the Malvinas.

The 1982 war ended with an Argentinian surrender after 74 days of conflict that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops, as well as three Falkland Islanders.

Buenos Aires has doubled down on its claim over the Falkland Islands after US President Donald Trump said Washington was open to reviewing its historically neutral stance on the territory.

London maintains the islands are British and rejects the jurisdiction of Argentinian courts in the Falklands.

The islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain British.

But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing that the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by Britain after 1833.

title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
excerpt:
As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all bro...
body_text:
As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.

But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.

From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.

The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.

Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.

“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”

The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.

Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.

Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.

But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.

“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.

“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft
excerpt:
Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for rare shrill carder bee

It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men an...
body_text:
Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for rare shrill carder bee

It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese.

But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way.

The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee.

Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything.

“You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.”

The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow.

Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.”

Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager with English Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.”

English Heritage rewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds).

The first group of scythers will help care for the meadow at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset, which was once a wealthy and important monastery with features including a thatched two-storey monks’ lavatory, which is unique in Britain.

They will work on a three-year project with the Bumblebee Conservation Trust to improve habitat for the shrill carder bee, a species that has declined significantly because of the loss of flower-rich grasslands.

As part of the project, English Heritage volunteers have been trained by the bumblebee trust to carry out wildlife surveys.

Rather than simply recording numbers, volunteers will monitor the relationship between bees and the meadow ecosystem, including which flowers are in bloom, which plants they are using, how far bees travel from their nests and how the habitat changes over time.

Hardy wrote about scything in prose and poetry: in Far From the Madding Crowd, Bathsheba Everdene watches haymaking, and the farm hand Mark Clark is described as “humming a tune to the strokes of his scythe”.

In his poem Four in the Morning, Hardy wrote about the “to-and-fro/Wheezed whettings of a scythe apace”.

The meadow at Muchelney is one of 100 that English Heritage pledged to create and enhance to mark the coronation of King Charles in 2023.

Slade said Muchelney was the pilot site but the idea was for the volunteers to travel to other English Heritage sites to use their skills. “We’re really at the beginning of this journey, but we’re very excited about it.”

title: Turkey detains dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and journalists
excerpt:
Protesters teargassed as minister claims widespread raids and arrests under obscenity laws were to ‘protect families’

Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a wave of raids...
body_text:
Protesters teargassed as minister claims widespread raids and arrests under obscenity laws were to ‘protect families’

Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a wave of raids and arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community, which has grown to include journalists as well as more than 150 arrested during protests against the raids.

Starting in the early hours of Sunday, Turkish police carried out simultaneous raids on the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organisations and HIV-advocacy groups in the cities of Istanbul, the capital, Ankara, and the coastal city of İzmir, as well as the cities of Aydın and Mersin.

“This is the widest crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch.

Video released by the Turkish interior ministry showed police rummaging through filing cabinets, grabbing rainbow flags and leading people away in handcuffs, as well as raiding nightclubs and the homes of activists.

Prosecutors in Istanbul said officials seized digital equipment, drugs and a firearm, as well as arresting dozens of people in the raids.

Rights groups tracking the arrests believe that 62 people have been held on remand, but more than 100 were detained. Sinclair-Webb, who accused authorities of attempting to smear and criminalise LGBTQ+ advocacy, said: “We believe this includes others not associated with LGBTQ+ groups [detained] for drug and prostitution offences.”

While homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey, prosecutors in Ankara have accused LGBTQ+ rights groups of violating laws prohibiting “obscenity”, and those governing NGOs, although formal charges remain opaque.

Turkey’s justice minister, Akın Gürlek, said the raids and arrests across the country were part of an operation entitled “My Family is Safe” and claimed the sweep was intended to “protect our children, the institution of the family and the social order”.

As a result, Gürlek said, authorities targeted venues they claimed were associated with prostitution, distribution of obscene material “and activities exposing children to such content”.

A Turkish press freedom group, the Media and Law Studies Association, said this included seven members of the executive board of Kaos GL, one of Turkey’s oldest LGBTQ+ advocacy groups that also operates a news site.

Tuğba Tekerek, a journalist, was arrested at her home in Istanbul and taken to Ankara for questioning by prosecutors, after publishing a piece with Kaos GL on the LGBTQ+ community in the neighbouring country of Georgia.

As the initial raids sparked protests, the wave of arrests grew this week. Turkish authorities teargassed hundreds of protesters in İzmir, and detained at least 150 demonstrators in Istanbul on Tuesday as well as dozens more in Ankara.

The French news agency AFP reported that several of the arrests outside a courthouse in Istanbul took place after demonstrators unfurled a banner that read “Being LGBTQ+ is not a crime” and chanted “Long live the struggle for freedom.”

A draft amendment to Turkey’s penal code that proposed prosecuting all LGBTQ+ people in Turkey for promoting behaviour “contrary to biological sex and general morality” was withdrawn last year.

Instead, the Turkish authorities have increasingly targeted LGBTQ+ individuals and groups using broad “obscenity” charges. Eleven leaders of the Genç LGBTI+ [Youth LGBTI+] organisation went on trial last month, accused of violating constitutional provisions on “family values” and publishing images showing same-sex couples kissing, charges that carry up to three years’ imprisonment.

The justice minister linked the launch of the “My Family is Safe” campaign to a directive launched by the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, declaring what he called “a decade of the family and population” and aiming to boost birthrates.

“Our family ties are weakening, the average age of marriage is rising, divorce rates are increasing and as a result, our fertility rate is declining. To be honest, the statistics are alarming for all of us,” Gürlek said.

But rights groups have questioned how arresting LGBTQ+ activists and demonstrators protects Turkish families. Sinclair-Webb said: “Obviously, protecting children and the family is important – no one is debating that – but in a country with a large and concerning record of domestic violence, many cases of child abuse and murders of women, the protection of the family cannot be focused on LGBT people.”

title: Prominent athlete tells Alan Jones trial he sent shirtless photo before unwanted kiss he wished ‘never happened’
excerpt:
Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app ...
body_text:
Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An alleged victim of Alan Jones has told a Sydney court that an unwanted kiss from the former shock jock more than a decade ago is seared in his memory and he wished it never happened.

The ex-sportsman, known as complainant M, agreed during cross-examination by the defence that he sent Jones a shirtless photo of him in Paris some months before the alleged kiss.

M explained the photo was sent in response to a question from Jones about how he was faring while he was overseas.

M replied “this good, haha”, accompanied by the photo which had just been taken of him, and which he thought was a good photo, the court heard on Thursday.

Jones replied: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up xxxxxx.”

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir suggested to M that the subsequent alleged kiss at an awards night in 2015 never happened. She showed him text messages where he was affectionate to the defendant despite testifying he was shocked and embarrassed.

“I know the kiss happened because I can’t get it out of my memory,” M replied on his third day in the witness box at Downing Centre local court.

“I wanted the kiss that happened to have never have happened. In some ways I feel as though I am deflecting [in the text messages].”

Jones has been charged with 20 counts of indecent assault an two charges of sexual touching against six men. He has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges.

Bashir on Thursday suggested that a text from Jones after the event which included the words “I hope you can feel my kisses darling” did not imply any kiss happened because Jones often spoke to him like that.

Jones had said: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after … You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

M replied with a message: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now. Thanks mate xoxo.”

M pushed back on repeated suggestions by Bashir that he has given conflicting statements to police and in court about the awards night when the alleged kiss took place. The defence barrister asked M dozens of questions about seating arrangements, the guest list, the timing of meals and awards and which direction Jones was facing when the alleged offence occurred.

“What I may not be able to give is who was sitting at my table ... at which direction something may have happened. Those things I may not recall,” the complainant said.

Bashir said in court: “I suggest the kiss allegation could not have happened in any location. You have never said in any police statement that this happened at the [location] have you?”

The trial is in its seventh week. The former athlete is the first complainant to choose to give evidence in a closed court and come face to face with Jones. The media were given permission to cover the case from a separate location.

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

title: US extends visa ban on Palestinian officials before UN General Assembly
excerpt: The United States Department of State has announced it will extend visa sanctions on officials of the Palestinian Authority (PA) and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), preventing ...
body_text:
The United States Department of State has announced it will extend visa sanctions on officials of the Palestinian Authority (PA) and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), preventing Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas from travelling to New York ahead of his address to the United Nations General Assembly next week for the second year in a row.

“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the State Department said in a statement.

The State Department accused the PA of violating US law by pursuing international recognition of Palestinian statehood outside direct negotiations, taking its dispute with Israel to international courts and providing payments to people the US and Israel label as convicted attackers and their families.

It added that the PA mission to the UN would keep a waiver under the UN Headquarters Agreement, which allows its regular staff to continue working even as individual officials are barred from entering the US.

Abbas’s speech this year had been expected to press for international recognition of Palestinian statehood and renewed momentum behind a two-state solution, following a wave of recognitions this month by the United Kingdom, France, Canada and other Western governments, as well as to draw attention to the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and the rapid expansion of illegal Israeli settlements and settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank.

No Israeli officials face equivalent US travel restrictions, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

Last year’s ban drew criticism from Palestinian officials and UN human rights experts, who said the visa bans breach the US’s obligation to allow individuals invited by the UN to travel to its New York headquarters, and have argued that singling out Palestinian representatives while shielding Israeli leaders undermines Washington’s stated commitment to a negotiated peace.

title: Yemeni forces target Houthis as US rules out direct role
excerpt:
US may be 'forced to intervene' in the Red Sea

The United States reiterated its support for Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Wednesday as fighting intensified between the Saudi-led co...
body_text:
US may be 'forced to intervene' in the Red Sea

The United States reiterated its support for Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Wednesday as fighting intensified between the Saudi-led coalition and Houthi forces. US officials also held direct talks with Houthi representatives in Oman last weekend, according to sources cited by Reuters.

Yemeni government forces said that the coalition had struck Houthi positions around Mocha and that government forces had launched drone attacks in Marib. The Houthis claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked regional and Western allies for help, according to two officials who spoke to The Associated Press news agency. The Saudis asked France, Pakistan, Egypt and the United Kingdom to deploy air-defence support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis. One official said Saudi Arabia’s main ally and arms supplier, the US, has seen its own stock of interceptors dwindle over the course of the war with Iran.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins told Al Jazeera that the US is “closely monitoring” the situation between Houthis and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen, adding that the US military has a longstanding “military relationship with our Saudi partners, and you see that manifesting today”.

Even as Washington assists the Saudi campaign, American officials held direct talks with Houthi representatives in Oman last weekend, according to three sources who spoke to the Reuters news agency on condition of anonymity. The meeting took place at the US embassy in Muscat with the assistance of the Omani government, two of the sources said.

At the Muscat meeting, the Houthis told US officials they had no intention of attacking US vessels and were committed to the 2025 ceasefire with the US, according to the sources cited by Reuters.

Meanwhile, the top US diplomat for Yemen, Neil Hop, told Yemen’s Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba that the US maintained its “strong support” for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, according to the US embassy in Yemen.

“The United States of America stands in solidarity with the Yemen government and its people against Iran-backed Houthi aggression,” the embassy said, citing Hop in a post on X.

The Yemeni government’s army said the Saudi-led coalition targeted Houthi outposts and equipment around the southwestern port city of Mocha. In a separate social media post, the government’s army also said they conducted drone attacks on Houthi forces in northern Marib governorate.

On Wednesday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said that “Saudi warplanes launched 40 air strikes targeting the provinces of Taiz, Marib and Hodeidah over the past 24 hours”. In response, the Houthis targeted the Khamis Mushait airbase and an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea port city of Yanbu, the group said in a statement.

The Houthis also claimed to have shot down a Saudi fighter jet using a “locally made surface-to-air missile” over the central province of Marib. Al Jazeera’s Yemen correspondent Yousef Mawry said the downing of Saudi fighter jets “could very well mean a change in the balance of power” as “Saudi Arabia depends heavily on its ability to carry out air strikes against Houthi positions in various provinces”.

title: Three dead after flooding inundates Navajo Nation in New Mexico
excerpt:
Indigenous authorities in the United States have said that three people have been killed in flooding in the southwestern state of New Mexico, where heavy rains left roadways blocked by water.

Navajo ...
body_text:
Indigenous authorities in the United States have said that three people have been killed in flooding in the southwestern state of New Mexico, where heavy rains left roadways blocked by water.

Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren said on Wednesday that police had responded to reports of people being swept away by floodwater at 12:30am (06:30 GMT) near the community of Newcomb in northwestern New Mexico.

Nygren said that two adults and a child were killed in the incident and offered condolences to the community, while advising residents to exercise caution in areas impacted by rainfall.

“There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a loved one so suddenly, and our hearts are especially heavy knowing that three lives were lost,” Nygren said. “To the family, relatives, and loved ones who are grieving today, we offer our deepest condolences. We pray that you are surrounded by strength, comfort, and the love of your family and community in the difficult days ahead.”

The National Weather Service (NWS) in Albuquerque, New Mexico, issued a special briefing on Tuesday warning of the possibility of widespread thunderstorms in the coming days. The service repeated those warnings on Wednesday, noting that moisture levels are expected to be at record levels for mid-September.

“A Flash Flood Watch is in effect for the western third of New Mexico and the South Central Mountains today,” NWS Albuquerque said in a social media post on Wednesday. “However, flash flooding could occur anywhere in central and northern New Mexico today.”

Heavy rainfall is predicted across parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah through Thursday. Flash flood warnings were issued for parts of northwestern New Mexico, along with flash flood watches for large areas of central and northern Arizona.

The deaths on Wednesday come several weeks after three hikers were swept away and dozens were rescued after heavy rainfall caused flooding at the Grand Canyon, a popular destination for tourists and outdoor recreation in Arizona.

title: Snapchat 'willing to implement' daily time limits for teens, boss tells BBC
excerpt:
Watch: CEO Evan Spiegel tells the BBC he would consider a time limit on Snapchat

The boss of Snapchat says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta f...
body_text:
Watch: CEO Evan Spiegel tells the BBC he would consider a time limit on Snapchat

The boss of Snapchat says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that he believed setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."

His comments came as the firm revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Evan Spiegel wearing the glasses at an event in June

Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses.

He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines.

"Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said.

Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world.

But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK.

"The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said.

The firm wants people to use the glasses for various tasks, such as streaming video, and says it can offer live translation across 60 languages.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

Smart glasses are 'an invasion of privacy' - Meta's are selling better than ever

The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public?

title: Israel and Morocco agree to open embassies, upgrading diplomatic ties
excerpt:
Israel and Morocco have agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties, including elevating their respective missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors to both countries.

A meeting between the two cou...
body_text:
Israel and Morocco have agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties, including elevating their respective missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors to both countries.

A meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers was hosted by the United States ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, in New York on Wednesday.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita also agreed to advance economic and trade relations, including completing two agreements by the end of this year on investment protection and preventing double taxation.

“[The] establishment of full diplomatic, peaceful and friendly relations between Morocco and Israel is in the common interest of both countries and will advance the cause of peace,” the US mission to the UN said in a joint statement on behalf of all three countries.

The two sides also agreed to expand air travel, including by reinstating direct flights operated by carriers from both nations, and confirmed plans for high-level bilateral visits in the coming months.

The announcement comes just a day after the sixth anniversary of the Abraham Accords, an initiative spearheaded by US President Donald Trump during his first term in office. The United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan have all joined the accords, which are aimed at normalising ties between Arab and Muslim-majority countries and Israel.

title: Young newlyweds killed after boat collides with water taxi and sinks in Venice lagoon
excerpt:

A pair of young newlyweds were ki...
body_text:
The State Department renewed its Level 2 travel advisory for The Bahamas, warning Americans about violent crime, unsafe boating conditions and other safety concerns.

A pair of young newlyweds were killed in a tragic accident involving a water taxi in Venice – just three months after they were married.

Gabriella Querino, 26, and Sean Michieli, 25, were killed Saturday morning in a collision involving a five-ton water taxi, Jam Press reported.

The couple was in a boat that had departed from Burano, an island in the Venetian Lagoon, about six miles northeast of central Venice.

BELOVED CRUISE SPOT WILL BE OFF LIMITS THROUGH 2027 AS SAFETY CONCERNS LINGER

They had set out to collect bait for Michieli's work as a clam fisherman.

Shortly afterward, the couple's boat collided with the water taxi — and sank.

Gabriella Querino, 26, and her husband, Sean Michieli, 25, were killed in a collision involving a water taxi in Venice. (Jam Press)

Querino was reported missing in the immediate aftermath of the crash as search efforts were hampered by strong currents and poor visibility.

Her body was eventually recovered from the lagoon.

Michieli was rushed to Venice-Mestre Hospital with severe head and facial injuries and other injuries across his body. He was pronounced brain-dead the next day.

CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING

Querino, originally from Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, moved to Italy about two years ago.

She developed a passion for fishing alongside her husband, who was from Cavallino-Treporti, Italy, according to Jam Press.

A five-ton water taxi collided with the couple's boat, which later sank in the Venetian Lagoon, according to reports. A stock image of a Venetian water taxi is seen above. (Alessandro Levati/Getty Images)

She was working to obtain the necessary license to join her husband in the fishing industry, according to the outlet.

The couple was expecting their first child, Italian newspaper Il Resto del Carlino reported.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Querino's mother, Gisele Elorriaga, told Brazilian media her daughter "was building a life for herself over there, and she was happy," Jam Press reported.

The young newlyweds, who were expecting their first child, were killed just three months after getting married when their boat collided with a water taxi. (Jam Press)

The exact cause of the collision remains unknown.

The water taxi driver is under investigation for nautical homicide as authorities work to determine the circumstances surrounding the collision, Italian news outlet Notizie.it reported.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Venice Public Prosecutor's Office for additional information about the investigation.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The tragedy comes amid a series of deadly boating incidents around the world in recent weeks.

Venice's waterways serve as transportation routes through the Italian city, where a water taxi was involved in a deadly collision. (Andrea Merola/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Last week, a passenger ferry carrying 47 people sank while traveling between two islands in Vanuatu, leaving at least one person dead and more than 30 others missing.

Just a few weeks earlier, a ferry carrying 267 passengers and crew capsized off northern Cyprus, killing multiple people.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: US military claims Strait of Hormuz remains open amid ongoing blockade
