Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as Ceta, with a broader “alliance for the future” aimed at creating “a common prosperity and economic security space”.

The commission president described that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values. “Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said.

“We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”

Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defence production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca
excerpt:
The Houthis denied they had targeted Mecca, where Islam's most sacred shrine is located

Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evenin...
body_text:
The Houthis denied they had targeted Mecca, where Islam's most sacred shrine is located

Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.

Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act".

The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".

But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies".

"There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.

Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.

He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.

There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour".

On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.

Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.

The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.

Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.

Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.

A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."

The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.

Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.

More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline

Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane

Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war

title: Mayors and other local leaders could be given powers to oversee water firms
excerpt:
Move would mean some input on companies’ spending and holding bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges

Mayors and other local politicians could be given powers to oversee water companies un...
body_text:
Move would mean some input on companies’ spending and holding bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges

Mayors and other local politicians could be given powers to oversee water companies under plans being considered by the UK government to bring utilities under greater public control.

Local leaders would have the power to direct some parts of water companies’ spending and hold bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges as part of the proposals.

It comes as Andy Burnham faces growing pressure to improve the oversight of the water industry, with millions of households facing steep bill increases, leaking infrastructure and sewage spills.

Giving local political leaders more authority over the sector was a key recommendation in Sir Jon Cunliffe’s landmark review of water companies last year.

The review found it would “represent a significant change, and ensure that local voices, customers and experts have stronger authority over companies’ boards’ decisions on investment priorities”.

These regional authorities could include a local government figure, a mayor, an independent chair, experts and other representatives to cover affected sectors such as transport and agriculture.

While there have been no firm decisions yet, officials in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs are keen on the idea, according to the BBC. It reported that the plan was among a number of ideas that the government was exploring to introduce greater public control of water companies.

Burnham has repeatedly promised to take public utilities into public control, including water companies. Before he became MP for Makerfield, he told the Guardian that he intended to nationalise Thames Water, the water company that serves 16 million customers and has been on the verge of collapse for more than two years.

At the end of March the regulated value of Thames’s assets was estimated at £23bn, while its net debt increased to £18.5bn. Ministers are considering whether to put the company into special administration or accept a solution put forward by creditors to maintain private sector control after a debt write-off.

In the meantime, customer dissatisfaction with the water industry has continued to grow. The number of complaints made by households about water companies is up 48% year on year, according to the Consumer Council for Water, the steepest annual rise in two decades.

Mike Keil, CCW’s chief executive, said the numbers reflect “just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector and the enormous task water companies face in rebuilding consumer trust”.

A government spokesperson said: “Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. We’re bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment.”

title: McLaren to build SUVs geared towards Formula One fans with children
excerpt:
Model comes as part of £500m UK investment by firm’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also fund new factory

McLaren is gearing up to build an SUV for the first time in its 63-year history, betting that ...
body_text:
Model comes as part of £500m UK investment by firm’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also fund new factory

McLaren is gearing up to build an SUV for the first time in its 63-year history, betting that the glamour of its all-conquering Formula One team can sell cars to wealthy fans who do not own its supercars.

The model, which does not yet have a name, comes as part of a £500m investment by McLaren’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also create 1,000 jobs, adding to the existing workforce of 2,500 people.

It will also fund a new factory, with Sheffield, home to McLaren’s existing carbon-fibre plant, understood to be the preferred site over the company’s headquarters in Woking.

Nick Collins, the carmaker’s chief executive, said the recent success of the McLaren racing team had created an “untapped love” for the brand among people who have never bought its cars.

The SUV would open the door to more buyers for whom two-seater sports cars were a limitation, he said. “It’s quite difficult if you have to decide which one of your kids you want to leave behind at home.”

The new model is part of a turnaround plan at McLaren Automotive, which was bought from the Bahraini sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat last year by CYVN Holdings, an Abu Dhabi government-owned investment company.

CYVN has vowed to invest $2bn (£1.4bn) in the loss-making group over five years. McLaren also merged with the British electric vehicle startup Forseven Holdings last April.

However, McLaren has no immediate plans to build an EV of its own, despite a government mandate saying all new cars in the UK must be zero-emission by 2035. “[Customers] are not asking us, and we’re not doing one,” Collins said.

Founded in 1963 by the racing driver Bruce McLaren, the company built racing cars, and later the McLaren F1 supercar in the 1990s, before spinning off McLaren Automotive as a dedicated road carmaker in 2010.

But it has struggled in recent years amid mounting debts and falling sales, before last year’s takeover by CYVN.

European luxury carmakers have faced tough trading conditions after a collapse in demand in China, a key market, which has already forced job losses at rivals Aston Martin and Bentley.

Michael Straughan, McLaren’s chief operating officer, said the SUV was a “critical” moment for the company, adding that he could “quite easily see us doubling” sales, which now stand at about 3,000 cars a year, through the new model.

He said the new factory was likely to be built in Sheffield, calling it “the jewel in the crown” for the company’s manufacturing capability, though no final decision has been made.

It comes amid a bumper period for sister company McLaren Racing, which has won the last two Formula One constructors championships and is also based in Woking. Mumtalakat still has majority control of McLaren Racing, while CYVN has a minority stake.

Straughan said: “There’s no doubt there’s people who are F1 fans … who would never purchase a McLaren sports car, but would definitely consider a McLaren SUV.”

He would not be drawn on the exact price of the new vehicle, but expects it to compete with the Bentley Bentayga, Aston Martin DBX and Lamborghini Urus, models that all start above £200,000.

“I think the trick here is conquest of other brands’ customers,” Straughan added – though not before seeing a Ferrari F40 drive past the window of McLaren’s technology centre in Woking.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, welcomed the investment, saying it showed the company was “doubling down on Britain”.

The growth of SUVs has come against the backdrop of warnings over “carspreading” and safety. Research has shown cars have grown 1.2cm longer, 0.5cm taller and 0.5cm wider each year on average since 2000, and that potential SUV buyers are undeterred by warnings they are more likely to kill pedestrians.

title: At least 12 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
excerpt:
Locals said 10 families had been living in the building despite warnings that it was unsafe

At least 12 people have been killed, including children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged buildin...
body_text:
Locals said 10 families had been living in the building despite warnings that it was unsafe

At least 12 people have been killed, including children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip, according to local rescue teams.

Video footage shows the search for bodies and survivors continuing in the rubble of the multi-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, its floors sandwiched together.

Locals said 10 families had been living in the apartments despite warnings that they were unsafe.

Members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence rescue service said they had initially been working with "empty hands" due to tight Israeli restrictions on equipment allowed into Gaza. However, they have since been able to borrow some heavy machinery.

On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.

The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.

Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza.

title: English village votes to leave UK in protest over migrant housing plan
excerpt:
Villagers in Piddington, Oxfordshire, hold symbolic referendum over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby

Residents of an English village have voted to leave the UK in a symbolic refer...
body_text:
Villagers in Piddington, Oxfordshire, hold symbolic referendum over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby

Residents of an English village have voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum against plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby.

The result of the poll in Piddington, Oxfordshire, was announced on Wednesday morning after 312 people voted on Tuesday. A total of 285 people were in favour of independence from the UK while 26 voted against. One ballot was spoiled.

The poll was organised by campaigners for residents to demonstrate opposition to government plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a converted Ministry of Defence site in the town of Bicester.

Reacting to the news, a government minister said she would “gently” tell residents of the village that the government was working to bring down the asylum backlog, and that a burden had to be shared across communities.

Lisa Nandy, the culture and media minister, told Sky News: “We are getting that backlog down. We’re speeding up the processing of claims, and in the meantime, we don’t think it’s acceptable for all of the burden of shouldering not just asylum accommodation, but also many other forms of temporary accommodation, to fall on poorer communities.”

She added: “That’s what we saw under the previous government. Because accommodation is cheap in many, not just towns, but in particular postcode areas. People who live in more deprived communities have had to put up with almost … every other house in some instances … turned into HMOs [house in multiple occupation], and that is not OK.”

The dispute over the plans in Bicester come against a backdrop of tensions elsewhere over the location of accommodation for asylum seekers. After disturbances in Thetford, Norfolk, earlier this year, which far-right activists attempted to exploit, the local Labour MP there voiced his concerns that cheaper, working-class areas were being chosen as locations for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.

Tim Bearder, the leader of Oxfordshire county council, said on Wednesday that the result in Piddington showed that campaigners had done “an incredible job” to highlight their concerns.

“This referendum shows how strongly they feel about the proposal and that is partly about the proposal itself and partly about way the government has gone about it, without engaging with local people and looking at the feasibility of the site,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

“It’s the wrong site for the local community and for the asylum seekers themselves,” said Bearder, who declined to say what alternative sites could be used.

The result was announced on Wednesday morning by a “returning officer” in front of an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall.

A parish councillor, Mike Nixon, said the proposed site had no pedestrian access areas, and that the nearest path was about a mile and a quarter away, down a busy unlit road.

The Home Office has previously said that the government is closing asylum hotels in what is expected to saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support and that it is working fairly to house asylum seekers across the country.

“As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area,” a spokesperson said.

title: Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci faces verdict for alleged war crimes
excerpt: The Kosovo war crimes tribunal will on Wednesday deliver its verdicts in the case of former President Hashim Thaci and several wartime commanders accused of murder and torture during the self-declared...
body_text:
The Kosovo war crimes tribunal will on Wednesday deliver its verdicts in the case of former President Hashim Thaci and several wartime commanders accused of murder and torture during the self-declared republic’s break from Serbia.

Thaci, 58, is facing several counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, torture and persecution, along with three former commanders from the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), a separatist militia that fought Serbian troops.

Thaci and the other former high-ranking commanders, Jakup Krasniqi, Rexhep Selimi and Kadri Veseli, deny the charges.

Prosecutors have requested 45-year prison sentences for each of the men.

The case is extremely contentious within Kosovo, where Thaci remains a revered figure for many Kosovan Albanians due to his role in the 1998-99 independence war.

On Saturday, tens of thousands gathered in the capital, Pristina, to call for their acquittal in the latest of several rallies since the trial began. Portraits of the four former KLA fighters have been plastered across the city along with a huge digital clock counting down to the verdicts.

“In the name of the people, declare them innocent,” one banner read.

According to prosecutors, the men targeted political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the KLA.

Thaci’s lawyers argued in February there is no evidence that directly links him to any of the crimes.

“There are no orders in the record from Thaci to perpetrators of crimes. There are no reports from perpetrators of crimes to Thaci,” lawyer Luka Misetic told judges at the Kosovo tribunal in February.

Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of NATO air attacks against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About one million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.

In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade refuses to recognise. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of negotiations mediated by the European Union.

title: Foreign students to face tough restrictions on bringing in family under Labor’s immigration plan
excerpt:
Home affairs minister Tony Burke will detail long-awaited changes as support for One Nation surges amid immigration debate

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new politica...
body_text:
Home affairs minister Tony Burke will detail long-awaited changes as support for One Nation surges amid immigration debate

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia, as the federal government shifts sections of the country’s immigration system away from demand-driven settings.

Long-awaited changes will be revealed by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, on Thursday, and are expected to include efforts to stop visa overstays and limit lengthy appeals processes for applicants.

The changes are designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy.

Burke will address the National Press Club in Canberra, with a speech titled “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”.

He had been due to announce the plans more than a month ago, but the speech was cancelled at the 11th hour amid debate inside cabinet about the direction and scale of the changes.

The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, allowing the government more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers, but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament.

“We do need to get net overseas migration down,” Burke said.

“We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy.”

Labor wants policy settings tweaked to ensure it can meet forecasts for Nom, as support for One Nation surges over concerns about rates of immigration.

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. Under the mooted changes, the vast majority of students would be required to come alone.

As well as 185,000 permanent arrivals annually, the government wants Nom to fall from about 305,000 to about 225,000 over two years, ending years of higher than expected arrivals, including from international students and working holidaymakers.

Nom measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months, including leaving and returning Australian citizens. Nom has fallen in seven consecutive quarters since September 2023. It is forecast to fall lower than pre-Covid levels by 2027-28.

But temporary visa holder rates remain high. For the 2024-25 financial year, there were 568,370 overseas arrivals, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.

Changes including efforts to stop people whose visas have expired from transferring to different categories are likely, essentially forcing some overseas citizens to leave the country more quickly.

The government is also expected to seek to drive down the number of unlawful non-citizens currently in Australia.

Department of Home Affairs data shows that, as of July, there were 110,898 individuals not granted a protection visa who were yet to be deported. The total includes people on bridging visas and others seeking a judicial or administration review.

Labor’s efforts to regain the initiative on immigration comes as One Nation surges in the polls and as community sentiment on the number of overseas arrivals remains a key issue motivating voters.

One Nation said on Monday it would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.

Business groups, universities, the aged care sector and both Labor and the Coalition all savaged the plan, warning Hanson’s proposals would hurt essential services and the economy.

Anthony Albanese tried to secure Coalition support for legislative changes in talks with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, last week, but no agreement was reached. The prime minister leaves Australia to attend the United Nations general assembly in New York on Friday.

The independent senator David Pocock said on Wednesday the country deserved a mature conversation about immigration, not one starting with numbers.

“The big thing I would love to see is a plan. There’s this constant talk about numbers, about classes of visas. Rather than actually having the conversation as a country, what is our 10-year plan for migration,” he told ABC radio.

“What are the skills that we need? What are the trade-offs when it comes to housing, impact on the environment?”

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, called for an end to “the race for the lowest Nom”, warning business needed skilled workers from overseas.

“We do not have a migration problem in Australia; we have a housing crisis and skill shortages. Those are the problems we need to fix. Shortsighted approaches that damage the economy won’t solve them. Those are red lines for business,” he said.

title: US military releases footage of massive operation to rescue injured airman stranded inside Iran
excerpt:
US military unveils dramatic footage of daring Dude 44 rescue deep inside Iran (Credit: U.S. Air Forces Central).

The U.S. military released dramatic new video on Tuesday showing parts of one of the ...
body_text:
US military unveils dramatic footage of daring Dude 44 rescue deep inside Iran (Credit: U.S. Air Forces Central).

The U.S. military released dramatic new video on Tuesday showing parts of one of the largest combat search-and-rescue operations in its history, including the moment elite Air Force pararescue operators reached a badly injured American airman stranded deep inside Iran.

The footage documents portions of the massive April operation to rescue the two-man crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle, call sign Dude 44, after the fighter was shot down by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile.

The pilot, known as Dude44 Alpha, and the backseat weapons systems officer, Dude44 Bravo, ejected from the aircraft and landed miles apart, leaving both stranded inside Iran.

While Dude44 Alpha was rescued after a little more than six hours, Dude44 Bravo suffered a broken back, arm and shoulder after a damaged parachute led to a hard landing. He remained stranded for nearly two days before U.S. forces reached him.

HOLLYWOOD LEGEND MAKING MOVIE ABOUT EPIC IRAN RESCUE MISSION TO SAVE F-15 FIGHTER JET CREW

Newly released U.S. military video shows Air Force pararescue operators reaching Dude44 Bravo on a mountain ridgeline after the injured airman spent nearly two days stranded inside Iran. (U.S. Air Forces Central)

The newly released video shows U.S. military helicopters searching for Bravo as American forces worked to locate and recover him.

Despite his injuries, Bravo moved away from his landing site and began climbing toward a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline as daylight revealed the desert valley and steep cliffs surrounding him.

The footage also shows American bombers and drones striking Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces that were in close proximity to Bravo.

TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS

U.S. military helicopters search for Dude44 Bravo during a massive combat search-and-rescue operation after his F-15E Strike Eagle was shot down over Iran in April. (U.S. Air Forces Central)

"There was clear intent out of the Iranian ground force to come find those two guys," Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine told CBS News this week.

The video then shows the dramatic moment on April 5 when two elite Air Force pararescue operators, known as PJs, reached the injured Bravo on the mountain ridgeline.

Two large search-and-rescue aircraft had landed on a makeshift desert runway before smaller "Little Bird" helicopters flew toward Bravo's position on the ridgeline.

Bravo called the moment he saw his rescuers "one of the greatest moments of my life."

HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY

Newly released military footage shows U.S. bombers and drones striking Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces near Dude44 Bravo as American forces worked to rescue the stranded airman. (U.S. Air Forces Central)

The second rescue operation put 92 U.S. service members on the ground in Iran, marking the first time American forces had boots on the ground in the country since 1980.

Hundreds of U.S. service members also supported the operation from the air, while between 3,000 and 5,000 service members supported the rescue mission overall, according to U.S. Central Command Commander Adm. Brad Cooper.

But the operation was not over once Bravo was reached.

The landing gear of the two rescue aircraft became trapped in the desert sand, stranding Bravo and more than 90 U.S. service members inside Iran. A clandestine Air Force unit was ultimately brought in to extract the group, CBS News reported.

Bravo was finally brought to safety roughly 50 hours after Dude 44 was shot down. The rescue was completed as the sun rose on Easter Sunday.

Two elite Air Force pararescue operators, known as PJs, reached the badly injured Dude44 Bravo on a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline inside Iran. (U.S. Air Forces Central)

Fox News' Liz Friden and Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Three killed after LA news helicopter crashes while covering deadly bus collision
excerpt:
Smoke and flames rise from Los Angeles fatal helicopter crash site

Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in...
body_text:
Smoke and flames rise from Los Angeles fatal helicopter crash site

Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in the city have said.

NBC Los Angeles confirmed the helicopter was its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, and was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash.

The station's hosts said both people on the helicopter, who were "valued friends and colleagues" had died, naming them as Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw.

They said the third victim was on the ground at the time of the crash, but did not name them.

The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson told the BBC.

Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD added.

During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed.

"We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said.

Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS: "We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed.

"That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said.

Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash.

Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported.

The helicopter crashed while covering a traffic collision involving an SUV and a city bus in Chatsworth

LAPD's Central Division posted on X that it extended "thoughts and prayers to the family, friends and colleagues of KNBC 4, Los Angeles".

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X she was "absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight".

"My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash," she added.

California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family".

"Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight."

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident.

title: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa
excerpt:
String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport...
body_text:
String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.

When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.

Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.

On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.

“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.

For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.

However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.

The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”

South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.

“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.

Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”

Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.

Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.

Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.

“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.

“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”

The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.

Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.

“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.

“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”

Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.

She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
excerpt:
Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?

The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in his firm and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to AI developme...
body_text:
Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?

The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in his firm and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to AI development, amid rising public concerns about the risks.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.

However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.

Speaking in Washington meanwhile, left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have both called for greater governance of AI.

Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.

"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, external every AI firm has the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety.

"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote.

"Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same Tuesday conference AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces.

"We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.

Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware.

Huang also argued  safety is an "engineering problem" and  companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product.

The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow, external and urge governments to regulate the industry.

The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk.

By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.

Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves.

"We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop".

Some political figures have pushed back against that view.

Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves.

Meanwhile, President Trump has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax".

Why doomsday warnings are not the only threat to the AI juggernaut

Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

Some industry figures have argued resurgent AI fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry.

During the conference, Altman addressed a crowd of hundreds of business people, telling them they should use AI tools to aid in their work, but also needed them in order to protect their businesses from potentially AI-enabled cyber attacks.

The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea.

Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks".

Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest, external.

"The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said.

"If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added.

AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC

AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act

Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.

Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.

He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.

"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.

OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.

"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

Do you have any comments or questions about this story?

title: US charges five people over alleged Russian plots
excerpt: Five people have been charged over alleged Russian intelligence-linked plots involving surveillance, recruitment and planned killings, according to an indictment unsealed by the United States Departme...
body_text:
Five people have been charged over alleged Russian intelligence-linked plots involving surveillance, recruitment and planned killings, according to an indictment unsealed by the United States Department of Justice.

Prosecutors said on Tuesday that the group worked on behalf of Russian intelligence services to carry out attacks and murders internationally, including within the US, and that all five remain at large.

The defendants were identified as Russian national Yuri Khrameev, 63, his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, Cubans Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both 35, and 22-year-old Venezuelan Angel Eduardo Castro.

All five were charged with conspiring to finance terrorism, while Khrameev, Suarez and Castro face additional charges of conspiring to commit murder for hire.

At a news conference, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the plots included attempts to kill a Russian dissident believed to be living in the Washington, DC area.

Justice Department officials said the network had recruited several people in the US to carry out surveillance on Russian dissidents, targeting individuals both domestically and in Lithuania.

In one instance, a recruit was reportedly promised $40,000 to make a US-based target “disappear”. A separate recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 the previous year to kill someone in Lithuania.

Russia’s embassy in the US has not commented on the case. Moscow has consistently rejected accusations that it has orchestrated assassination operations on foreign soil, including in the US.

title: Jeremy Greenwood denies giving ‘ridiculous’ evidence to Icac about ‘mum’s perspective’ from premier’s sister-in-law
excerpt:
Counsel assisting inquiry suggests Anita Perrottet’s alleged advice on vaping and greyhound industry was already on public record from other sources

A Liberal factional figure has rejected a suggesti...
body_text:
Counsel assisting inquiry suggests Anita Perrottet’s alleged advice on vaping and greyhound industry was already on public record from other sources

A Liberal factional figure has rejected a suggestion he gave “ridiculous” evidence that Dominic Perrottet’s sister-in-law shared in $660,999 for giving a “mum’s perspective” on lobbying clients, the New South Wales anti-corruption watchdog has heard.

Jeremy Greenwood told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Wednesday it was not relevant that Anita Perrottet’s children were under five at the time she provided advice on vaping among minors.

Greenwood also denied he gave false evidence about her coming up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” several years after it appeared in a greyhound industry report.

Icac is investigating an allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from fugitive developer Jean Nassif, or his company Toplace, in exchange for political outcomes.

Greenwood, who alongside Charles Perrottet has denied payments were political donations, returned to the commission on Wednesday after Nassif made an explosive video appearance from his Beirut bedroom on Monday and Tuesday. Nassif declared he was “not corrupt”.

Peggy Dwyer SC on Wednesday questioned Greenwood in relation to his previous evidence about advice he said Anita Perrottet gave to lobbying firms Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.

Dwyer has alleged invoices of $660,999 paid to Anita Perrottet’s company, Macquarie Consulting, over two-and-a-half years were her husband Charles Perrottet’s share of the money from Nassif.

Anita Perrottet has told the watchdog payments were for “strategic and marketing advice” she provided; while Charles Perrottet has said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif on his developments as well as his wife’s work.

Greenwood has previously told the commission Anita’s advice, for which the commission has no written evidence, provided a “mum’s perspective”. He said after first being contracted by Beckington in 2020, she may have come up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for greyhounds, and given advice about discouraging minors from vaping, including removing flavours such as bubblegum, as well as black market regulation.

On Wednesday, Dwyer took Greenwood to 2017 recommendations by the NSW greyhound industry reform panel, which included the phrase “zero unnecessary euthanasia”, suggesting to Greenwood he had “outsmarted [him]self by coming up with that false evidence when it’s clearly a term used in a document years earlier”.

“I disagree,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer showed Greenwood a submission by Philip Morris to a 2020 senate inquiry which referenced measures to regulate the illicit tobacco trade and a 2019 report committing to applying guidelines to prevent youth access to vapes.

Greenwood said he had read the submission by Philip Morris, a client of his, but rejected Dwyer’s suggestion it “makes a mockery” of his evidence about Anita Perrottet’s advice.

After Dwyer asked him how old Anita Perrottet’s children were at the time she provided advice on vaping, Greenwood said he did not know, and did not think it was relevant.

The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened to tell Greenwood he was “not here to debate with counsel assisting” but to “answer the question”. Greenwood said: “I presume they’re under 10.”

Dwyer, telling Greenwood that Anita Perrottet’s children were around two and three at the time, asked: “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?

Dwyer said: “Your evidence is ridiculous, can I suggest to you, that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.” Greenwood disagreed.

At the inquiry last week, Greenwood acknowledged an arrangement under which payments to Macquarie Consulting would also remunerate Charles Perrottet for advice he gave to Nassif.

He rejected a suggestion he gave false evidence at private private hearings with Icac every year between 2023 and 2026, in which he did not mention an arrangement. But on Wednesday, he said he had never been in a financial arrangement with Charles Perrottet for consulting work, but said they had previous arrangements “on a racehorse” and “an old Redfield [college] rugby fantasy football league”.

Dwyer said it was a “ridiculous response” given his previous acknowledgement “that an amount going to Macquarie Consulting was in effect to thank Charles or compensate him for the advice he had given to Jean Nassif”. Greenwood disagreed.

Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year and is not expected to appear. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

title: Saudi Arabia warns of ‘red line’ after Houthi drone intercepted close to holy city of Mecca
excerpt:
The Iran-aligned militant group rejected the suggestion it had targeted Mecca, while the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned the attack

Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and destroyed...
body_text:
The Iran-aligned militant group rejected the suggestion it had targeted Mecca, while the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned the attack

Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, according to a ⁠spokesperson for the ⁠Saudi-led ​military coalition which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen.

The security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”, ⁠coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the ⁠Houthis.

Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest ​city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims ‌undertake each year.

Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, after what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017.

A Houthi official rejected the claim on Wednesday, with spokesperson Hazem al-Assad writing on X: “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.”

The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned what they called a “heinous” attack on Islam’s holy city, blaming the Houthis. The group – which is made up of 57 Muslim-majority countries decried the “ongoing aggression against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.”

Saudi Arabia issued security alerts across parts of the country on Tuesday, including in Mecca and other ‌cities, following a week of attacks by Iran-aligned fighters that have drawn the kingdom deeper into the Middle East ​war.

The US embassy issued an advisory to “reconsider travel” to Saudi Arabia after the alerts in Mecca and other areas amid Houthi attacks. The advisory warns of the “risk of Iranian drone and missile targeting of American interests, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans and local laws regarding social media activity,” adding “Do Not Travel to the Yemen border due to threat of terrorism.”

The Houthis have seized control of parts of ⁠Yemen’s Red Sea coast overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, one of the ​world’s most important ​shipping straits, threatening Saudi oil ​exports rerouted from the strait of Hormuz.

The group has ​announced several major ‌attacks on ​Saudi Arabia over ​the past week, including strikes on an airbase on Monday that it said were retaliation for airstrikes on Yemen.

title: Stephen A. Smith calls out NBA star Kawhi Leonard for letting Clippers take the fall for salary cap scandal
excerpt: On this episode of Don’t @ Me with Dan Dakich, Dan breaks down the high-stakes, hostile homecoming as LSU prepares to walk into a wall of noise against Ole Miss. From Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry ca...
body_text:
On this episode of Don’t @ Me with Dan Dakich, Dan breaks down the high-stakes, hostile homecoming as LSU prepares to walk into a wall of noise against Ole Miss. From Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry calling for military backup to Kiffin admitting there are legitimate "safety issues" awaiting him on the sideline, SEC football culture is on full display. Dan dives into why Kiffin insists his players have nothing to worry about, how he's shifting all the game pressure onto the Rebels, and why this is easily the most anticipated narrative of the college football season.

ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith went nuclear on Kawhi Leonard after the Los Angeles Clippers' salary cap scandal, torching the league's soft punishment for a guy who just packed his bags back to Toronto.

"For him to cause all the trouble that he's caused for this organization and to walk away with nothing more than having to surrender $700,000 worth of restitution is a crime," Smith said on First Take. "Kawhi Leonard … he's a gangster."

The NBA dropped the hammer on the Clippers with the most brutal penalty in league history: a $30 million fine, five lost first-round picks, and a one-year suspension for owner Steve Ballmer.

LOS ANGELES CLIPPERS FINALLY GIVE UP ON KAWHI LEONARD, SEND FORMER FINALS MVP BACK TO TORONTO RAPTORS

Investigators blew the lid off a shady scheme using sponsors like Aspiration and Daktronics to route millions in under-the-table cash to Leonard and his uncle, Dennis Robertson. The mess even triggered federal and SEC probes, plus a five-year NBA ban for Robertson.

Stephen A. Smith speaks on stage as he and Christopher Russo host SiriusXM shows live from Fanatics Fest at Javits Center on July 17, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images for SiriusXM)

Los Angeles Clippers forward Kawhi Leonard, right, looks toward the scoreboard during the second half of an NBA basketball game in Inglewood, Calif., on May 1, 2025. (AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill, file)

Yet Leonard got off with a lousy $700,000 fine, zero suspension, and a ticket straight back to Toronto.

CLIPPERS FACE FEDERAL CRIMINAL PROBE AFTER NBA PUNISHES TEAM OVER KAWHI LEONARD DEALS

Smith spelled out how Leonard let management take the bullet while he skated away untouched.

"He broke the rules, got caught, pointed the finger at somebody else, threw the organization under the bus, got his money and left the country," Smith said. "I mean, [expletive], how much better can it get than that?"

SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 06: ESPN reporter and analyst Stephen A. Smith is seen on the set of "First Take" on February 06, 2026 in San Francisco, Calif. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) (Getty Images)

Despite federal and SEC probes into the illicit side deals, the NBA let Leonard walk with a $700,000 restitution fee. In the end, it was a minor handling charge for a guy clearing nearly $50 million annually. He even waived a $7.45 million trade kicker to guarantee his exit back to Canada.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Clippers got hit with $30 million in fines, surrendered five first-round picks, and lost their owner for a year. Meanwhile, Kawhi blamed his inner circle, claimed total ignorance and hopped on a flight to Toronto without missing a single game.

Smith got this one dead right: Kawhi pulled off the ultimate hustle.

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Alice Springs heavy metal music venue raises $1m in donations in fight to stay open
excerpt:
Supporters from around Australia back the Black Wreath, a volunteer-run centre far off the beaten touring track

Alice Springs has a population of 34,000 and exactly one dedicated live music space: a ...
body_text:
Supporters from around Australia back the Black Wreath, a volunteer-run centre far off the beaten touring track

Alice Springs has a population of 34,000 and exactly one dedicated live music space: a heavy metal venue called the Black Wreath. It has hosted hundreds of bands from around the country over the past decade – despite being 1,500km from the nearest city.

For musicians in central Australia, the Black Wreath is a one-of-a-kind resource. So when its operators were informed last year of the owners’ plans to sell, they negotiated a stay of execution and began devising a fundraiser that could save the desert venue. A month-long crowdfunding campaign, which called for donations that would let the team behind the Black Wreath buy the venue and place it in a trust, hit its $1m target on Friday.

The Black Wreath’s founder and creative director, a lip-pierced and leather-clad man known mononymously as Pirate, says it feels surreal to have raised so much money for what is a DIY, volunteer-run venue far off the beaten touring track.

“I haven’t quite processed it,” he says. “We’re feeling very overwhelmed and a lot of gratitude.”

Pirate says the $1m arrived in donations from $20 up to $10,000 and came from supporters around Australia. The grand vision is to use the money to keep the Black Wreath alive to give musicians from central Australia a space to perform, “and for Alice to be a touring destination for other artists year-round”.

But the work is not done yet. Pirate says the successful Pozible campaign is just “step one” towards securing the Black Wreath’s future and that “there’s multiple ways that could unfold”. He still has to negotiate with owners, who have an asking price of $1.23m on the venue – a sum higher than the amount the fundraiser collected. Pirate wants to secure additional funding through philanthropy and by “reaching out to some of the biggest bands in the world”. The Black Wreath is still gratefully accepting donations, and has set a new fundraising target of $1,111,111 – a nod to the date of the Black Wreath’s inception: 11 November 2011.

The fundraising campaign comes two years after the Tote, some 2,300km away in Melbourne, crowd-sourced $3m to keep itself open.

The Black Wreath was born out of the desire “to put Alice Springs on the map” and “create something that is available as a resource for the entire town”, Pirate says.

“I grew up playing in bands with my friends here, and we were extremely limited with pathways and opportunities – no one nationally recognised this place as a heavy music town,” he says. “There was not much we could do with it. There weren’t any studios, venues or rehearsal rooms.”

A collective of three bands founded The Black Wreath as a record label and a series of backyard studios, before later leasing what was then a run-down industrial building and turning it into a creative hub complete with a recording studio, rehearsal spaces and stage. The collective expanded and now operates a national heavy music festival, Blacken Open Air, which takes place in April and May one hour outside Alice Springs.

Pirate believes the reason the town has such an affinity for heavy metal stems from “the isolation of the place – small-town frustration”.

“Growing up with lack of opportunity and a lot of energy, you just identify with metal,” he says. “Metal is a global community. And young people, when you discover that, it makes you feel part of something bigger … [especially if] you already feel like you’re disconnected from the world”.

While the Black Wreath was born out of a love for metal, Pirate says the venue serves “every genre of music” and the entire Alice community: “Young people. First Nations communities. The queer community. The headbangers and the rockers and the punks, and also the doofers and the hip-hoppers.”

But the challenges of running a music venue in one of the most isolated locations on Earth are plentiful, especially given that it only sells alcohol – where most venues make the bulk of their income – “a few times a year”, to cover production costs at select, bigger events.

“The expenses of doing it are higher than anywhere else in the country,” Pirate says. “The cost of travel for bringing artists out here is just astronomical … for the last decade or so, it’s been a struggle.”

Pirate works as a volunteer and doesn’t draw a wage from the Black Wreath, instead propping it up with income from his various day jobs. The venue is operated “purely for the love”, he says.

He hopes the success of the fundraising venture inspires others to fight for live music.

“It is a tough time for the music industry,” he says. “And I just hope that people can see the real power of community – the power is in our hands. We can do something about it, and keep fighting to uplift live music.”

title: Sally Field remembers shopping at Walmart with Dolly Parton: ‘Can you imagine all of us?’

Sally Field told Fox News Digital after her Emmy Award win on Monday night that she "never" stopped loving Dolly Parton.

Sally Field remembers shopping with Dolly Parton at Walmart like it was yesterday.

After the Emmy Awards on Monday night, Field took a moment to remember her loving friendship with the late country music icon and trips they used to take to their local Walmart.

"She was a friend. I admired her. I loved working with her. I never stopped loving her. There were moments where we tried to reach each other, but you know, this is a weird world I live in, this acting world where you do films, and you're so bonded with this group of people, it's like being in battle together," Field told Fox News Digital.

Sally Field honored Dolly Parton at the 78th annual Emmy Awards.
 (Adam Scull/PHOTOlink/Courtesy Everett Collection )

"It's like being in battle of the bulge together, and you save each other's lives, and you've got each other's backs, and you spend 24/7 with each other, and we would go shopping together, all of us, and go to Walmart together," she continued. "Can you imagine all of us coming into Walmart? And it never leaves your soul."

Field explained that she lived far away from Parton, so getting together was a struggle for the two.

Julia Roberts, Sally Field, Shirley MacClaine, Dolly Parton, and Daryl Hannah all appeared in "Steel Magnolias." (Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images)

title: Fourth Florida resident dies after contracting flesh-eating bacteria linked to oysters
excerpt:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel warns beachgoers about the rise of Vibrio vulnificus, a deadly flesh-eating bacterium found in warm salt waters.

A fourth person in Florida has died af...
body_text:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel warns beachgoers about the rise of Vibrio vulnificus, a deadly flesh-eating bacterium found in warm salt waters.

A fourth person in Florida has died after contracting flesh-eating bacteria commonly linked to consuming raw or undercooked oysters, health officials said.

The death was included Thursday in the Florida Department of Health's updated fatality count for the deadly flesh-eating bacterium Vibrio vulnificus.

The individual was from Broward County and between the ages of 75 and 79, WSFA reported. It remains unclear exactly how the person contracted the infection.

Previous deaths were attributed to residents of Bay, Palm Beach and Marion counties, according to the state’s health department.

BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE

FILE — Florida health officials warned that eating raw or undercooked oysters can lead to infection with Vibrio vulnificus, a flesh-eating bacterium. (iStock)

"Most people get vibriosis by eating raw or undercooked shellfish, particularly oysters," the Florida Department of Health said.

According to the department's website, Florida has reported 21 cases of Vibrio vulnificus in 2026.

In the last 10 years, 2022 and 2024 reported some of the highest numbers of cases and deaths in the region. Florida recorded 19 deaths and 82 cases in 2024, while 2022 saw 17 deaths and 74 cases.

North Carolina mountain community braces for hurricane season two years after Helene's brutal impact

Officials said the unusual increase stemmed from certain counties experiencing impacts from hurricanes Helene and Ian. Severe weather events that cause standing or floodwaters pose a risk of exposure to the bacteria, officials said.

Vibrio vulnificus is a naturally occurring bacterium found in warm, brackish seawater.

POPULAR BEACHES CLOSED AS HIGH BACTERIA LEVELS RAISE HEALTH CONCERNS FOR SWIMMERS

FILE — Vibrio vulnificus bloodstream infections are fatal about 50% of the time, according to Florida health officials. (CDC.gov)

Exposure can occur when a person eats oysters contaminated with the bacteria or enters contaminated water with an open wound.

Health officials said bloodstream infections caused by Vibrio vulnificus are fatal about 50% of the time.

While healthy individuals typically develop a mild illness, Vibrio vulnificus infections can cause severe illness in people with weakened immune systems.

"A recent study showed that people with these pre-existing medical conditions were 80 times more likely to develop Vibrio vulnificus bloodstream infections than healthy people," Florida health officials said.

'I THOUGHT I HAD THE FLU': MOM NEARLY DIED AFTER DISMISSING DEADLY SEPSIS SYMPTOMS

FILE — In this aerial view, a person walks through floodwaters that inundated a neighborhood after Hurricane Milton came ashore on Oct. 10, 2024, in Punta Gorda, Florida. Flooding and standing water can increase the risk of exposure to Vibrio vulnificus, health officials said. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Severe infections can cause symptoms including fever, chills, decreased blood pressure, also known as septic shock, and blistering skin lesions. In some cases, wound infections can lead to tissue damage requiring amputation.

Elsewhere along the Gulf Coast, Louisiana has reported 15 cases and six deaths this year as of Sept. 9, according to the Louisiana Department of Health. Fourteen of the cases were attributed to wound or seawater exposure.

The Texas Department of State Health Services says Texas typically sees an average of 33 cases per year.

Mississippi reported three cases as of August, according to the state’s health department.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: The Palestinian school under siege – podcast
excerpt: At least five pupils at a village school in the West Bank have been killed in the last year by settlers and soldiers. Emma Graham-Harrison reports on how the school found itself on the frontline, whil...
body_text:
At least five pupils at a village school in the West Bank have been killed in the last year by settlers and soldiers. Emma Graham-Harrison reports on how the school found itself on the frontline, while a teacher explains what life is like for staff and students.

Waheed Abu Naim is an English teacher at the Al Mughayyir boys’ school in a village in the West Bank. He loves his job, he says. “I am happy to be a teacher. Although we don’t get lots of money, because my students, especially in the morning, wait for me when I enter the school to shake hands, to smile at me while going inside their classes. So it’s a happy life.”

But the last year has been anything but happy for Waheed. His village is now surrounded by settlers, while the military has blocked off every road except one, which has a checkpoint on it. Teachers who live in neighbouring villages cannot always come to work. But worse are the attacks on the village by settlers.

In April, a 14-year-old pupil was killed next to a playground gate after a gunman opened fire. As Waheed rushed the teenager to hospital he learned his own brother had also been killed.

Senior Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison tells Annie Kelly: “We’ve documented the hundreds of children who’ve been killed by Israeli soldiers, settlers over the last three years. But even in that context, of sort-of regular deadly violence, there is something particularly horrific about someone taking aim at a school full of children.”

Four other students were also killed and, says Emma, things don’t seem to be getting better. “In the next few months I’m just, very unfortunately, expecting to see at least the same level of violence and frankly, probably an escalation.”

As the WNBA searches for its next commissioner, Sophie Cunningham said she has spoken several times with current NBA commissioner Adam Silver, who is in charge of the search for the league's next leader.
